t: for the tithe of the children of Israel. And the continuation of the verse: 'which they raise up to the Lord as a gift, I have given to the Levites as an inheritance'.

2. and everywhere that it says of the tithe 'sacred' or 'redemption'. Everywhere in the Torah that language of 'holy' and the law of redemption is mentioned in connection with tithe (see Leviticus 27:30-31, Deuteronomy 14:25, 26:12-13; Yad Pashut).

and your gift will be reckoned to you etc.. This verse was said to the Levites regarding the terumah of the tithe that the Levite gives to the priest from the first tithe, and the verse equates the terumah of the tithe with the great terumah, and the first tithe with the unconsecrated produce from which the great terumah is separated.
like the grain from the threshing floor. Like the first of the grain (great terumah) that is separated from the threshing floor (the place where the grain is threshed).
and like the fullness. Ripe grapes.
first tithe from which its terumah was taken. From which the terumah of the tithe was separated.
who was taken captive. Who was taken captive by gentiles, and there is concern that they had relations with her.
they give her the tithe and she eats. Unlike terumah (see Hilchot Terumot 6:7-11).

the Sages penalized her so that she is forbidden to eat tithe. Since she did not investigate properly whether her husband had indeed died (for other penalties they imposed on her see Hilchot Gerushin 10:7).
they separate first tithe. Even though they do not give it to another person, they must separate first tithe from their produce.
they take from everyone. They receive terumot from Levites and Israelites, and give none at all.
by oral tradition. The Sages' tradition in interpreting the verses.
the tithe. First tithe.
who did not go up with him to Jerusalem. From the Babylonian exile, at the beginning of the Second Temple period (see Ezra 8:15).
the tithe in its tevel state. Before the terumah of the tithe was separated from it.
for they are liable to death at the hands of Heaven. Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:19.
to their owners. To one of the priests.
you have nothing in them until they are raised up. The priests and Levites have no right to the gifts until they are separated.
a person is permitted to eat as he goes along at first. To eat of the produce while it is still tevel, with the intention to separate afterward (see also Hilchot Bikkurim 5:12).
and he need not tithe from what is adjacent. From nearby produce (unlike the great terumah, which is taken only from what is adjacent; Hilchot Terumot 3:17).
but one does not tithe from one kind for another kind etc.. Similar to the great terumah (there 5:2-3, 5:12).

everything we said about terumah etc.. The law of tithe is like the law of terumah regarding separating on produce of a different kind, ab initio and after the fact, as detailed in Hilchot Terumot chapter 5.
and anything exempt from terumah. Produce from which one need not separate (Hilchot Terumot 2:9-12).

and whoever may give terumah may tithe etc.. Whoever is permitted to give terumah ab initio is permitted to tithe. And whoever should not give terumah ab initio but whose terumah is valid after the fact, so too with respect to tithe (there chapter 4).
through you. On your behalf.
he need not stand etc.. And likewise he need not ask him afterward whether he tithed, since the agent volunteered to tithe on his own and we assume he did so.
and if he said to his fellow, tithe on my behalf. If the owner of the produce asked his fellow to tithe for him, and he agreed.

he must stand with him. Or ask him afterward whether he tithed, since there is concern that his agreement to tithe stemmed from embarrassment and was not wholehearted, and therefore this agreement cannot be relied on until the matter is verified (Radbaz, Derech Emunah).
by their word. By the word of the Sages.
carobs etc.. This speaks of a particular variety of carob that is a poor variety and not very fit for human consumption (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:3).

for a fig tree standing in a courtyard, one is obligated to tithe its fruits if he gathers them together. If he picks two figs together in a courtyard he must tithe them (as below 4:15), and it is proven from this that there is an obligation of tithes even in a place not defined as a field, for a courtyard is not designated for sowing as a field is.

onions that took root next to each other. Onions detached from the ground that were placed together, and because of moisture passing from one to the other they continued to sprout and grow (Yad Pashut).
in the soil of an upper room. On the roof of the house, where soil is found.

exempt from tithes. Since they are as if planted in the house and are not obligated by the Torah, and the Sages did not obligate them in this case either, since he is not interested in their taking root (Or Sameach, Torat Kohanim Pshuta, Ma'aserot p. 702).
a collapse fell on them and they are exposed. The roof of the upper room in which the onions were placed fell and now the onions are exposed to the air (ibid.).
the figs that remain in that field. The time for picking the figs has passed, and a few figs remain in the field.
cucumber and gourd fields. Fields of cucumbers and gourds.

therefore they are subject to tithes and terumah. For they are in the category of 'human food that is guarded' (Hilchot Terumot 2:1), and are not ownerless, even though the field is not guarded because of them.
one tithes only from the choicest. One must separate the good fruits for tithe (see also Hilchot Terumot 5:1).
as it says. Regarding the terumah of the tithe.
its best part. The good part of it (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 7:5).
for the tithe that the Levites separate. The terumah of the tithe, which is a tenth of the first tithe that the Levite receives.

one does not tithe by estimate. By estimation and guess, since the measure of the tithe is stated explicitly in the Torah and it is forbidden to deviate from it (as with the terumah of the tithe, and unlike the great terumah; see Hilchot Terumot 3:4, 3:10).
rather by measure etc.. Each thing in the manner in which it is customarily measured (see there 3:11).
by measure. A volume measure.

his tithes are spoiled, for tevel is mixed with them. For the produce in excess of the tithe measure did not take on the status of tithe but remains tevel as before, so there is a mixture of tevel and tithe.
and his produce is rectified. For tithe was separated from it.
part of the tithe. Less than the measure.

it is tithe only as one who divided the heap. The status of tithe did not take effect on it and the produce remains tevel, unless he divided the produce and separated from one part the measure suitable for that part (some versions read 'only like one who divided the heap', meaning that such a separation is considered only as dividing the heap of tevel in two. Similarly in Hilchot Terumot 3:7: 'it is like one who divides the pile').

but he must separate from this portion from which he took out his tithe etc.. The tithe he must give for the portion he separated (which is tevel) must be separated from those same fruits and not from other tevel fruits. Since at first he separated these fruits with the intention that they be tithe, he must separate the tithe from them (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Terumot 4:1, Hilchot Terumot there).
tithe from the tithe. The terumah of the tithe.

to separate tithe. The term 'ma'aser' is used here as a general name for terumot and tithes, and so in all laws concerning the obligation of tithes in general (such as when the obligation begins, as detailed in the rest of this chapter and in the following chapters) - the terms 'ma'aser', 'ma'aserot', or 'to tithe' include terumot and tithes.

one who finishes his produce to eat it himself. One who completes the tasks done to the crop (as detailed below 3:8 onward) with the intention of eating it, he and his household (and see below 3:1-3, 4:1-2, that the obligation by the Torah applies only when he brought the produce into the house after completing its processing).
the buyer. The purchaser.
unripe grapes. Grapes that are not ripe.

it is permitted to eat from them as much as he wishes and in any way he wishes. For before the tithing season no obligation of tithes applies at all. And after the tithing season it is forbidden to eat a fixed meal but still permitted to eat a casual snack until the produce's processing is completed (below 3:1).
cucumbers. Muskmelon, resembling a large cucumber (based on Commentary to the Mishnah, Kil'ayim 1:2).
for they are left only to increase their size. They are left attached to the ground so that they become larger, and not in order to make them ready for eating.
their emergence. Their sprouting.
once the fruits are able to be sown and sprout. That their seed can be sown and other fruits will grow from it.
everything according to its fruit. Each fruit in its own time.
so that they are fit for eating etc.. That if he picks them and leaves them, they will ripen by themselves within twenty-four hours.
once the berry is crushed. The grape is mashed.
once they swell like leaven. They soften and swell like bread that has leavened (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:2).
peaches, once they show red veins. That the peach has stripes of red color (like veins).
once the flesh separates from the outer shell. From the time the nut's fruit separates from the hard outer shell.
but dates are exempt always. As above 1:9.
pine cones. The fruit of the cedar (Bavli Avodah Zarah 14a).
and lot. Apparently chestnuts or pine nuts (based on Commentary to the Mishnah, Shevi'it 7:5, explaining the word 'lotem').
and batnim. Pistachios (Commentary to the Mishnah there).
when they are finished. When their ripening is complete.

and this is their third. This is what the Mishnah says (Ma'aserot 1:3): 'once they have brought in a third', meaning that a third of a log of oil can be pressed from a se'ah of olives, and when the olives are fully ripe three logs of oil can be pressed from a se'ah (Commentary to the Mishnah, Shevi'it 4:9, based on his reading in the Jerusalem Talmud, Shevi'it 4:7).
once they become round. Once they take the shape of a fruit (Derech Emunah).
the og. The buckthorn, a tall wild shrub on which clusters of small red fruits grow.
once they turn red. Once they begin to redden.
once they make black dots. Before they blacken completely.
pears and crustumel. Some identify them as different varieties of cultivated pear, and some identify them with plums and apricots.
and prishin. Quinces.
and uzrarin. A light-colored fruit resembling a small apple, growing on the thorny azarole shrub.

once they make white bald patches. These fruits are covered with fine hairs, and at the beginning of ripening the hairs begin to fall and in their place a kind of white bald spot appears, until all fall off when ripening is complete (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:3). Some explain that the bald patches refer to light spots that appear gradually on the surface of the fruit during ripening, until the fruit becomes completely light (Rabbi Yisrael Pelix there).
once it brings a third. The grains will reach a third of their growth.
fenugreek. Fenugreek.
and gourds. Bottle gourd, called kara in Aramaic and Arabic.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 4.
that it has reached. The tithing season.

the whole side. The whole side of the vineyard, for one grape is a sign that all the vines on that side will soon reach the tithing season, and their law is as if they had reached it (Radbaz, Aruch HaShulchan 95:10).
a berry. A grain.
all of it is connected. The whole side is obligated in tithes as with a cluster of grapes (Kesef Mishneh); some explain that only the seeds of that pomegranate are obligated (Aruch HaShulchan there).
he may not sell... to one who is not trusted regarding tithes. Since he causes him to stumble in a prohibition.
and if some ripened early. If some of the fruits advanced earlier in the growth process.

and it is permitted to sell the rest etc.. For when the prohibition is not present now (but will only be in the future), the Sages did not worry about causing a stumbling block to one who is not trusted (Aruch HaShulchan 95:11, Derech Emunah).
its pomace. The olive waste.
its grape skins. The grape peels.
its straw. The grain waste.
wine lees etc.. Lees of tithed wine from which he wants to produce additional wine.

if he put in three and found four, he removes tithe for this excess. If the quantity of liquid increased so that the addition is a quarter of the present quantity (for example, he soaked the lees in three liters of water, and after straining the lees found four liters), the liquid has the law of wine (see Hilchot Berachot 8:9, Hilchot Shabbat 29:15). And since when he tithed the original wine he separated only for the wine in it, he must now separate tithe for the lees that have now become wine (Ramban, Bava Batra 96b).
from another place. From other wine, since if he wished to separate from the mixture he would have to separate for the mixture of water and wine and not only for the extra wine.
for one who separates terumah initially has in mind everything. When one separates great terumah, which has no measure by the Torah, he intends to exempt also the wine absorbed in the lees.
as we have explained regarding terumah. Hilchot Terumot 4:21.
if he found less than four... exempt. For there is no wine here at all.
one who consecrates his produce. To the property of the Temple.
and redeemed them. He bought them from the Temple treasury (and the sanctity passed from the produce to the money he gave for them).

the treasurer. The official in charge of the consecrated property; and since the produce was in the possession of the Temple treasury at the time of the obligation in terumot and tithes, they are exempt (see also below 3:25).
their processing was not completed. The tasks in the field were not completed.
and threshed it. He separated the kernels from the husks.
he did not winnow it. He did not scatter it in the wind to remove the remaining waste.
and did not smooth it. Smoothing is leveling and beautifying the heap of grain (see below halakhah 13).
it is permitted to eat from them casually. As explained below halakhah 19.
and one of six things fixes for tithes. These things give importance to the eating of the produce, and from here on any eating from them is considered a fixed meal and is forbidden.
cooking. With fire.
he brought cucumbers and gourds into the house before he rubbed them. Which is the completion of their processing, as below halakhah 8.
from a basket of figs. A basket of figs.
before its processing was completed. Before he covered it or before he filled all of it (as below halakhah 10).

it became fixed for tithe. Since placing in a vessel confers a certain importance, and sometimes it is the final task for the produce. Therefore when he places in a vessel and in addition takes from it, the two matters combine to fix it for tithe.
fig branches. Fig branches.
date palm fronds. Date palm branches.
they were not fixed for tithe. By the law of one who brings into the house before the completion of processing (above halakhah 4).

and if the householder brought them in, they are subject to tithe. For it is assumed that he intends to use the fruits while still attached to the branches (for example, to serve them thus before guests), so these fruits reached completion of processing before they were picked (Radbaz).
were not fixed. For their processing was not yet completed.
to eat them as meleilot. Ears of grain that one crumbles by hand and chews.

in what case? with grain; but with legumes etc.. Types of grain are customarily eaten as meleilot, and therefore one who brings them in for that purpose is like one who completes their processing, since they are ready for eating for him. But with legumes this manner of eating is not customary, and therefore his intention has no effect in the matter.
and to bring it in with its chaff. To bring it into the house before separating the waste, for the house does not fix before the completion of processing as above halakhah 4.
so that his animal can eat. For an animal can eat together with the chaff.
and he winnows little by little etc.. If he wants to eat himself, he may take a little grain, separate the waste from it and eat it, and afterward take a little more grain.

for he is not beginning to finish everything. He does not intend to winnow all the grain and complete its processing in the usual way, but only to winnow a little for immediate eating (unlike what was stated above in halakhah 4, that beginning an act of completion on produce brought into the house fixes it for tithe immediately).
these became tevel for tithe. They are forbidden as tevel, having become fixed for tithe (for the reason for the law see Piskim veShitot).
in the drying area. A place where fruits are spread out to dry.
watermelon beside watermelon. Watermelons are not made into a heap so that they not crush one another (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:5).
who finished all his need. Who rubbed all the fruits he wants now.

their processing was completed. Of the fruits he wants now (and in halakhah 4 above the case is after he brought them into the house, therefore even if he rubbed only one, all became obligated; Riaz, Kesef Mishneh, and Radbaz, and see there where they brought an additional distinction between the cases).
even though he did not remove the yellow from them. Because it depends on his intention, and some eat without removing the yellowing (explanation of the Tosefta, Lieberman edition, Ma'aserot 1:6).
the vegetables that are bundled. That are customarily arranged in bundles.
if he does not fill. If he does not intend to fill the vessel to the end or he gathers into his hand.
and with fronds. Palm leaves.
it becomes tevel. Since he completed the tasks done in the field.
the berries. The seeds taken out of the pomegranate to dry them.
one who smooths the face of the heap. Who levels and straightens the pile.
with a rachat. A kind of large flat spoon.
at the end of everything. At the end of the tasks done on the grain.
once he sifts. Once he cleans them of waste by means of a sieve (a large sifter).

and takes from under the sieve and eats. He collects the legume seeds that fell through the mesh along with the waste (Rabbi Yisrael Pelix, Ma'aserot 1:6, and see there another explanation). They are permitted to eat since their processing was not completed.

from the fragments. Crop that scattered from the stack and gathered in another place (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:6). Some explain that this refers to cut ears that were not threshed (Rash and other commentators).
and from what is inside the straw. That has not yet been separated from the waste.
and eats. A casual snack, for all of these were not in the heap and smoothing did not apply to them.
and he may remove the grape skins and seeds. He may remove the peels and pits.
the pit. The place where the wine gathers before being placed into jars.
the upper winepress. The place where the grapes are trodden.
and from the channel. Through which the wine passes from the winepress to the pit.
to the ukah. To the hollow where oil gathers after being pressed.
the akel. A round basket made of ropes in which olives are piled for pressing.
the memel. A stone for grinding olives.
and from between the pasin. Between two stones or two beams of the olive press.
and to the tamchui. A vessel in which a cooked dish is placed after cooking.

because it does not cook in a second vessel. Oil is not cooked (and therefore not fixed for tithe) when placed in a hot dish in a second vessel (the first vessel is the vessel in which the dish was cooked, and the second vessel is the vessel to which the dish was transferred).

because it is cooked. When the dish is very hot, even though it is in a second vessel, it makes the food fit for eating and gives importance to eating it, and therefore it is considered cooking for the purpose of fixing for tithes (Radbaz, Chazon Ish, Ma'aserot 4:18; unlike the law of cooking on Shabbat, see Hilchot Shabbat 22:6).
a cake of figs. Pressed figs.
once he smooths it. Once he makes the cake smooth and attractive (with a smooth stone, or by smearing fruit juice; see the commentators on the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:8).
dried figs. Dried figs.
once he packs them. Once he stores them densely in a vessel.
into the storehouse. Into a storehouse (a depot or large vessel).
once he rounds them with his hand at the mouth of the storehouse. Once he arranges and smooths the outer dried figs.
he may not eat until he tithes. For they have already been fixed for tithe.
that are in the drying area. A place where fruits are spread out to dry.
for their processing was completed etc.. For he revealed that the drying does not hold him back.
before he gathered them to the top of the roof. That he spread them on the roof to dry, but has not yet gathered them into one heap (which is their completion, as above halakhah 12).
he takes some of them down for the animal. Which is accustomed to eat fresh carobs.

because he returns etc.. For he has not turned his attention away from the drying, and so the carob processing was not completed (unlike one who takes from the drying area and carries to another place as stated above in halakhah 17).
who preceded him with the ears. Who separated first tithe before great terumah when the grain's processing had not yet been completed.

before he separated his terumah. Before the Levite separates the 'terumah of the tithe' for the priest. For fruits called 'first tithe' become immediately obligated in the terumah of the tithe by virtue of their name (Bavli Beitzah 13b), even in grain whose processing has not been completed (but the Levite need not separate great terumah, as stated in Hilchot Terumot 3:13).
lashes for rebellion. Rabbinic lashes.
rubs. Peels by rubbing with his fingers.
tosses from hand to hand. Shakes and passes from hand to hand so that the husk comes off.
in his bosom. In the folds of his garment.
into a cold dish. That does not cook.
the pot. A kind of pot.
because it is like a small pit. For the pot gives importance to the wine and fixes it for tithe, like a small pit containing clean wine ready for drinking (Aruch HaShulchan 100:3).
but not into his hand. He may not fill his hand with oil in order to anoint his body with it.
and if they were completed... he may not declare ownerless. For he has already become obligated in terumot and tithes.
bundles of straw. Thin bundles of a little fine straw.
cuttings. Detached fruits.
these are exempt from tithe. Since he acquired them from ownerless status before their processing was completed.
they pressed them. They packed them into vessels (which is the completion of their processing, as above halakhah 16).
slices of a cake of figs. Pieces of a round cake of figs.
for it is known that they come from something completed. For the cake is cut after its processing is completed.
krichot. Small, light bundles of ears of grain.
in a private domain he must tithe. For they are not ownerless and must be returned to their owners (see Hilchot Gezelah vaAvedah 15:10), and therefore they are subject to tithes.

in the public domain they are exempt. For in the public domain the owners despair of them because they roll from place to place, and the finder acquires them (there 5:8), and therefore they are considered ownerless before the completion of processing, which is exempt from tithes.
but sheaves are subject to tithe everywhere. Heavy bundles that remain where they were placed even in the public domain, and the finder must return them to their owners (there 5:10).
smoothed grain. Whose processing was completed (as above halakhah 13).
he makes it terumah and tithes for other produce. He separates from it for other produce that is subject to tithes.

and he does not worry. He need not worry that it was already separated from (in which case he would be separating from the exempt for the obligated; see above 1:6), since terumah is generally separated only when the grain is uprooted from the place where its processing is completed (Jerusalem Talmud, Ma'aserot 3:1), and here the case is that he found the heap of grain in the place where it was smoothed (Derech Emunah, Yad Pashut).
a covered basket. Whose processing was completed (as above halakhah 10).
he found a basket. That is not covered (Derech Emunah).

in a place where most bring into the market, it is forbidden to eat from it casually. For fruit whose processing was completed with the intention of selling in the market may not be eaten casually (above halakhot 1-2; and in an uncovered basket the processing is completed when he fills it or gathered all he needs, as above halakhah 10).

and he rectifies it as demai. He separates from it part of the tithes in the manner that one separates from fruit bought from an am ha'aretz (see below 9:1-5), lest the owner of the basket be an am ha'aretz and did not tithe the fruit properly.
and in a place where most bring into houses, he eats from it casually. For they were not fixed for tithe until brought into the house, as above halakhah 2.
and rectifies it as certain. Since the fruit in it was not yet fixed for tithe, and we assume it was not tithed.
half and half. Half of the people bring to the market and half to the house.

he rectifies it as demai. For there is concern that it belonged to a person who brings to the market and it became obligated in tithe, and therefore it is forbidden to eat from it casually and must be rectified out of doubt that the owner is an am ha'aretz and did not rectify it properly.
and if he brought it into the house he rectifies it as certain. He separates all the tithes, lest it belonged to a person who brings into the house and the fruit has only now been fixed for tithe.
in what case is this said. That when most bring into houses he must separate all the tithes.

in something that has no completion of processing. That no special act is done to complete the processing, such as an uncovered basket (mentioned above), whose processing is completed at the end of the ordinary work and not by a special act (Derech Emunah).

but with something that has a completion of processing etc.. When a special act is done to complete the processing (such as smoothing a heap or covering a basket), it is customary to separate great terumah at the completion of processing. Therefore when he finds a covered basket that was uprooted from the place where it was made, he need not separate great terumah.
ant holes. Holes in which ants store grains.
that lodged. That stayed there at night.
for from something completed. Whose processing was completed.
one who finds olives etc.. This halakhah, continuing the previous one, deals with a person who finds his own crop within his own property.
for they change and become soiled with dust. And one cannot tell whether they fell from the tree above them or from elsewhere.
perhaps they fell from this fig tree. And so they are untithed.

or from figs that were tithed. Or these figs came here from tithed figs in the courtyard. And so these figs are of doubtful tithing status, and because of the doubt he must rectify them (Even HaAzel, Mar'eh HaPanim, Ma'aserot 3:2, and see Hilchot Gezelah vaAvedah 15:15 regarding a case where the fig tree leans toward the road; and see Kesef Mishneh, Radbaz and other commentators who explained in other ways).
and redeemed them. He redeemed them from the Temple treasury.

are exempt from tithes, for at the time of their obligation they were exempt. See also above 2:8 regarding one who consecrates attached produce. The rule that emerges from combining the two halakhot is that if the produce is in the Temple treasury's possession at the tithing season (when attached) or at the completion of processing (when detached), it is exempt from tithes.

and one who consecrates standing grain for meal offerings is exempt from tithes. Although meal offerings are not brought from tevel (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:9), when he consecrates the grain while it is still attached it is exempt from tithes (since at the time of completion of processing it belonged to the Temple treasury), and is fit for the meal offering (see Tosefta Menachot 10:7).
I have removed the sacred from the house. I removed all the tithes from the house, and gave them as required (this verse is said in the tithe confession, see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni veNeta Revai 11:7).
the gate. The door of the house.
by way of roofs. Such as through the chimney in the roof, and also through a window in the wall of the house.
and karpifot. A yard behind the house from which one can enter the house, but which is not the main entrance (Derech Emunah).
as they explained by oral tradition. As the Sages received by tradition that this is how the verses cited in the previous halakhah are to be learned.
in the other six things we counted. In the other possibilities among the six mentioned above 3:3.
lashes for rebellion by their word. Rabbinic lashes.
as we explained that one who completes etc.. Above 2:1.
four cubits. About two meters.
does not fix. For it is not considered a house.
for example, if the house was sloped and rising. If the walls of the house or their upper part are built diagonally inward, so that the area of the roof is smaller than the area of the house
this roof is like part of the airspace of the house. For it has no independent importance but is considered part of the house and fixes for tithe like the house.
the tzrifin. A structure made of two slanted walls of reeds that touch each other at the top (in a triangular shape).
and the burganin. Watchtowers.
for it is found without walls. And is not fit for living in during the rainy season.

the outer potters' hut. Used for making and selling earthenware vessels. Inside it there is another hut used for living, which fixes for tithe as below halakhah 10. [Note: the Rambam in the Commentary to the Mishnah vocalizes the word tarnegolin as 'tarnogelin'.]
and a festival sukkah. The festival of Sukkot.

they make tevel for their owners. They fix for tithe with respect to the person to whom they belong, who is there more than others and for whom it is considered a permanent residence (see Derech Emunah).
a school. Where Scripture is taught to children.
and a study hall. Where Mishnah is taught to adults (Yad Pashut).
and a house of Talmud. A house where people gather when needed to discuss matters of halakhah, and in which they are not present regularly all day (Radbaz).
if they have a residential dwelling. If they serve as human living quarters.
the uriarot and the storehouses. Kinds of storerooms (see Torat Kohanim Pshuta, Ma'aserot p. 691). Some explain that uriarot are horse stables (Riaz).
for storage. For storing grain.
and if they were for living. If they also serve as a person's residence.
by way of the gate. And not over the fence or through a back door through which fruit is not customarily brought (Derech Emunah, and as above halakhah 1 regarding the house gate).
a courtyard with two residents. That has two houses in it and two tenants live in it (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 3:5).
that belongs to two partners. Who are partners in the house in the courtyard.
a gatehouse. A booth adjacent to the gate of the house in which the gatekeeper sits.
and the portico. The area before the house that has three walls and a ceiling.
both fix. That the outer one too is considered a guarded courtyard even though those entering the inner one pass through it.
the potters' hut etc.. Explained above halakhah 4.
one who carries his fruits from place to place. Who wants to eat them at the place he arrives at.
entered with them. Entered with the fruits.
to the place that is the end of his journey. To the final destination where he wants to eat the fruits as a fixed meal.
and likewise on the return. For example, if he decided to return to his home and eat the fruits there (Kesef Mishneh).
peddlers who go around the towns. Who go around different towns to sell their goods.
eat casually. From fruits that the residents of the courtyard give them (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 2:3).
until they reach the house where they lodge. Which is considered their home.
in a courtyard exempt from tithes. As explained above halakhah 8.
he is permitted to take them out and eat from them casually. For a house fixes only when he brought the fruits in knowingly.
and likewise if he forgot and took them up to the roof. Through the house.
eats from them casually on the roof. For the passage through the house was done by forgetfulness, and he may eat on the roof itself since a roof does not fix, as above halakhah 3.
to his fellow's courtyard. A guarded one.

they became fixed and he may not eat until he tithes. This speaks of one who decided to eat the fruits in his fellow's courtyard. For although he brought them into the courtyard by forgetfulness, since he now decided that this will be the place where the fruits are eaten, even his fellow's courtyard fixes (Rabbi Yosef Kafih, and see other commentators who found the Rambam's words difficult and emended them).
a courtyard that is hoed. That was hoed for planting.
it is like a garden etc.. The law of a residential courtyard that fixes for tithes is nullified for it, and its law is that of an agricultural area where casual eating is permitted.

and if he sowed most of it, one does not eat in it casually. The commentators found this law difficult, since sowing is a more advanced stage in turning the place into an agricultural area. One explained that when he hoes most of it he will certainly end up hoeing all of it, but when he already sowed most of it and did not complete, he reveals that he does not intend to sow the rest and does not intend to turn the place into an agricultural area, and it should be assumed that the sown area too will eventually be uprooted (Penei Moshe on the Jerusalem Talmud, Ma'aserot 3:4).
and if he planted a courtyard for ornament etc.. Planting for ornament is not considered planting for this purpose, and the law of a hoed courtyard therefore returns.

eats from it one at a time and is exempt. He picks one fig from the tree and eats it, since a courtyard fixes for tithes only crops whose processing is completed (above 3:3), and picking one fig is not considered completion of processing (Radbaz below halakhah 18, Chazon Ish, Ma'aserot 6:4).

and if he combined, he is obligated in tithe. If he picked two figs together this is like completion of processing, and it is forbidden to eat them even casually, for a courtyard fixes something whose processing is completed.
his bosom. The folds of his garment.
for the airspace of the courtyard does not fix for tithe. And it is permitted to eat casually from something whose processing was completed before it was fixed for tithe (above 3:2).
and leans toward the garden. The branches of the fig tree enter the airspace of the garden.
he eats from it in the garden as usual. A person standing in the garden may eat many figs casually, since these figs are not in the courtyard and were not fixed for tithe.
he may not take the entire cluster and eat. For cutting the cluster is considered completion of processing, like the law of one who combines two figs in halakhah 15 above.
picks grape by grape. He picks one grape from the cluster attached to the vine and eats, and then picks another grape and eats.
breaks apart the pomegranate on the tree. Takes out seed after seed while it is still attached to the tree.
the berry. A single seed.
he sofet it etc.. He eats from it with his mouth (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 2:6); some explain that he cuts thin pieces from it (Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura, Ma'aserot 3:9).
and he entered from the garden into the courtyard. Intentionally (and if he forgot and entered, see above halakhah 13).
coriander. Field coriander, a spice plant now called kusbara.
nibbles. Cuts.
the buyer. The purchaser.
detached fruits. Whose processing was completed in the seller's possession (as above 2:2).
they were fixed for tithe by rabbinic law, as we have explained. For a purchase fixes for tithe as above 3:3, and its obligation is rabbinic as above 4:2.

once he gives the money, even though he did not pull. For from the time of payment the sale takes effect by the Torah (Hilchot Mekhirah 3:1). And although the Sages enacted that as long as he did not lift the produce to acquire it he may retract and receive his money back (there halakhah 4), for the purpose of fixing the produce for tithe it is considered a sale from the time of payment.
selects and sets aside. Chooses fruits from among the fruits in the store and sets them aside to buy them afterward.

even though he decided in his heart to buy, he did not become obligated to tithe. Even if he decided to buy them he is not obligated as long as he did not perform an act of acquisition on the fruits (see also below 11:8).
and if he was God-fearing etc.. Who wants to fulfill what he decided in his mind even though it has no force as a monetary acquisition.
he tithes. He separates from the fruits he wanted to buy and gives the seller the cost of the tithes, or separates the tithe from his own fruits.

were not fixed. For a purchase fixes for tithes only when he buys detached fruits whose processing was completed for his own consumption (for the Sages enacted fixing by purchase in a manner similar to fixing by the Torah, and by the Torah the obligation of tithes is only when he intends to eat them himself, as above 2:1; Shach, Yoreh De'ah 331, subsection 119).
one who buys attached to the ground. A person who bought fruits not yet picked.
here, take this issar and give me five figs for it. Take a coin and give me five figs in exchange, and this speaks of figs whose processing was not completed (Riaz).
and if he combined, he is obligated to tithe. For combining is like completion of processing (as stated above 4:15 regarding a courtyard).
for twenty figs that I will select for myself. That I will choose and pick for myself from your fig tree.
he selects one at a time and eats. For in this way the sale is of something whose processing was not completed, as explained in the previous paragraph.
grains, berries, sofet. See above 4:17 for explanation.

for he acquired only what is picked. Since he said that the acquisition will be of those fruits he selects, the sale takes effect only after he picked the fruits, and therefore if he picked them in a way that is considered completion of processing, the sale fixes for tithe.
for these twenty figs. That are attached to the ground, where the sale takes effect while they are attached.
cuts as he likes. Even many figs together.
one who exchanges with his fellow. Fruits for fruits.
this one to eat and that one to eat. Each of them intends to eat the fruits he receives, and is considered a buyer for eating.
to spread out. To spread out to dry.
as we have explained. Above 3:3.

both are exempt etc.. The one who gathers twenty figs is considered a buyer (for he pays for them by giving his fellow permission to fill his belly from his own), and the reason he is exempt is that he gathered from attached produce whose processing was not completed. And the one who fills his belly is not considered an exchanger (whose law is that of a sale) but is considered a recipient of a gift (for he may eat more than the number of figs he allowed his fellow to gather), and therefore he is exempt even if he took from fruits whose processing was completed.

and if he combined and ate, he is obligated. The one gathering twenty figs, who is considered a buyer, must eat them one at a time as above halakhah 3, and if he combined he is obligated because it is considered completion of processing. But the one filling his belly, who is considered a recipient of a gift, is exempt even if he combined, since it is permitted to eat casually from something whose processing was completed and has not been fixed for tithe (Riaz).
and a gift does not fix as a sale. It does not fix for tithes as a sale (some versions read 'like a sale', with the same meaning).
they eat. Casually.
for a gift does not fix. And this speaks of a place where most people bring into houses, in which case the fruits were not fixed for tithe upon completion of processing (Derech Emunah).

if most of the people bring into houses. If most people in that place are accustomed to take home the crop that grows in their field, we assume that this am ha'aretz too does so, and gave them figs that had not yet entered his house and had not been fixed for tithe.
they tithe. For these figs became obligated in tithe from the time they entered the houses of the people who received them as a gift.
bring to the market. They carry their crop for sale.
they rectify only demai. They separate tithes on the basis of doubt (see below 9:2-5).

perhaps he tithed and afterward brought to the market. For fruits meant for sale are fixed for tithe from the completion of processing in the field (above 3:1-2), and an am ha'aretz's fruits that became obligated in tithe in his possession are of doubtful tithing status (below 9:1).
and if he said, take for yourselves and bring into your houses. From this statement it implies that in his claim the figs are tithed (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 2:1).

he tithes as demai. Even if most people bring into houses, since we assume that these figs entered the house of the am ha'aretz and were already fixed for tithe (for he testifies about them that they are tithed, and before bringing into the house it is not customary to tithe). However, an am ha'aretz is not trusted about all tithes, and therefore one must tithe as demai.
a large quantity. A large quantity of figs.
it is as if he said to him: take and bring in. For a large quantity is generally not eaten outside, and giving such a quantity is like a statement that these figs are tithed.
something not usually eaten raw. A fruit or vegetable that needs cooking inside the house, and therefore it is considered as if he said 'take and bring in'.
this one eats and is exempt. The person who was told 'take and eat' may eat casually in the market without tithing.

and this one eats and is obligated. The second person is obligated to tithe even if he wants to eat casually in the market, since we assume that the fruits he received were fixed for tithe in the am ha'aretz's house (as above halakhah 6).
in the gate. A gatehouse of a courtyard, which fixes for tithes like a courtyard (above 4:9).
they eat. Casually.
and we have already explained. Above 4:11.
when the fruits pass through it. When his fellow's house is not the final destination for the fixed eating of the fruits.
to work with him. To work for him.

since they may eat by the Torah from what they work on etc.. By the Torah, workers are permitted to eat while working from the fruits they work on, when they are engaged with detached fruits whose processing was not completed or with attached fruits at the completion of their work on the attached produce (Hilchot Sekhirut 12:1). Therefore their eating the fruit is not considered a sale, as it does not stem from a monetary agreement but from the command of the Torah.

that his son eat from his wages. That his son eat in his place; and without a condition he may not give his share to his son, even though he does not cause the householder a loss, since the Torah gave the right only to the worker himself during his work (there halakhah 13).

that he eat after the completion of his work on detached produce. For without a condition he may eat from detached fruits only when he works on them before the completion of their processing (there halakhah 2).
since he eats because of his condition. For his eating stems from a monetary transaction he made with the householder.
and the worker stipulated that he eat olives. For without a condition he does not eat, since weeding is not the completion of their processing while attached (there halakhah 4).
he eats etc.. By the law of a buyer in halakhah 3 above, so that if he combined it is completion of processing and the sale fixes for tithes.
and stipulated to eat vegetables. The green leaves of the onion.
nibbles. Cuts.

the worker fixed that he would eat a ratla of olives. A worker engaged in work in which the Torah permitted those working on it to eat without limit. But here the worker agreed with the householder that he would eat a fixed quantity. And he may eat this quantity whenever he wishes, unlike an ordinary worker, who is permitted to eat only during the work (Derech Emunah).
ratla. A litra, a unit of volume.
dip. Dip.
for they were fixed by the salt. For salt fixes for tithe as above 3:3 and below halakhah 18.
working on lavsin. Working on a poor variety of figs (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 2:8).

he may not eat bnot sheva etc.. He may not eat from another variety of figs on which he is not working (Hilchot Sekhirut 12:10), and if he received permission from the householder to eat from another variety - he must tithe like a buyer.
bnot sheva. A choice variety of white figs (Commentary to the Mishnah there).

but he may etc.. He may refrain from eating the poor fruits he works on, and eat his fill of the choice fruits of that variety he works on, and need not tithe since he eats by Torah law (see also Hilchot Sekhirut 12:11).
to do work for him in the field. This speaks of work in which they may not eat from the crop during the work, such as plowing or reaping (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 3:2).
when they have no food provision from him. That he did not obligate himself to supply them food for the workday.
they eat from the fruits in the field and are exempt from tithes. If he gave them permission to eat they need not tithe, for a gift does not fix for tithes as above halakhah 6.

provided their processing was not completed. The commentators found this condition difficult to explain, since a gift does not fix even for something whose processing was completed (see Derech Emunah). Perhaps it should be explained as referring to fruits that the owners intend to take to the market (or where the worker does not know the owners' intention), in which case they are fixed for tithe immediately upon completion of processing as above 3:1-2.

for one does not pay a debt from tevel. For it is forbidden to sell untithed produce (see below 6:6), and paying a debt is like a sale (there halakhah 9). And when he obligated himself to provide the workers food and they eat from tevel, it is like paying his debt from tevel.

rather they eat one at a time from the fig tree. They pick a fig and eat, and then pick another fig, for in this way, where the fruits have not yet been fixed for tithe, the Sages permitted paying one's debt from tevel (Derech Emunah).

but not from the basket etc.. For after completion of processing the fruits were fixed for tithe by the sale (for when the householder obligated himself to provide food, the workers have the law of a buyer).
the basket. A large basket.
the drying area. A place where figs are spread out to dry.

the one who parboils. Cooks lightly in water without spices (Rabbi Yosef Kafih's note to the Commentary to the Mishnah, Berachot 6:8; and see Commentary to the Mishnah, Terumot 10:11, Hilchot Nedarim 9:1). Some explain that 'shaluk' means cooked a lot (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and elsewhere; and see Meiri there, that the word is explained in both senses, all according to context).
one who smokes the fruits until he makes them fit. Raises smoke under the fruits to make them fit for eating.
one who buries fruits in the ground etc.. In order that they warm and soften there.
were not fixed for tithe. For burying is not considered cooking for tithes.
into a pot or an alpas. Cooking vessels.
when they are boiling. When they contain a hot dish that was cooked in them on the fire (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:7, and see above 3:15).
they were fixed for tithe. The wine or oil are considered cooked and were forbidden to eat casually.
he mixed. He diluted.

even in the winepress. Even in the place of treading grapes before their processing is completed, since cooking (or putting the wine into a vessel) is considered completion of processing (and also fixes for tithes, like cooking something whose processing was completed).
and the shachalayim. A plant with sharp green leaves.
they became tevel for tithe. Since grinding makes them fit for eating and is considered completion of processing and fixes for tithes.
it was fixed. For creating a drink is like cooking.
the tamchui. A bowl containing a cooked dish.
it was not fixed. Since he did not create a drink that stands on its own.
one who cracks. Opens.
the sap. A milk-like fluid.
exempt. For sap is not considered a drink.
the ma'atan. A place where olives are piled so that they soften before pressing (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 4:3).

terumah after which a second must be given. For example, if he gave terumah from a non-perforated pot on a perforated pot, which they considered terumah, but the fruits are still tevel for terumah and he must give terumah a second time (see Hilchot Terumot 5:14-16).
they were fixed for tithe. By the first terumah, although it did not rectify the fruits.
and the eve of Shabbat darkened on them, they were fixed. Since at the onset of Shabbat everything is designated and ready for eating (Commentary to the Mishnah, Terumot 8:3).
children. Children.
they may not eat at the end of Shabbat until they tithe. Although on Shabbat eve they may eat (commentators based on the Jerusalem Talmud, and see the next halakhah).
fig tree. A fig tree.
basket. A basket.

he may not eat until he tithes. Even on Shabbat eve, for fruits designated for Shabbat are fixed for tithe immediately. And in the previous halakhah they were not fixed before Shabbat, since they were designated for Shabbat by children who have no understanding (Radbaz).
he may not finish his eating etc.. Even though he began permissibly.
one may smooth figs and grapes of tevel. It is permitted to smooth with the hand a cake of stuck-together figs and also stuck-together grapes (Commentary to the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:8).
and there is no loss in this. There is no concern about spoiling the tevel, although the smoothing makes the fruits rot faster (ibid.).
and whatever is forbidden to non-priests to eat of terumah, of the pits and the peels etc.. See Hilchot Terumot 11:10-13.
so it is forbidden. To every person.
and from tithe from which terumah was not taken. From first tithe from which the terumah of the tithe was not separated.
and from second tithe... that were not redeemed. For it is forbidden to eat second tithe outside Jerusalem unless one transfers its sanctity to money (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1-2).
they do not light with it. They do not use it as fuel.

and needless to say on the Sabbath. For the needs of the Sabbath. Some explained that Sabbath lamps are more stringent in this respect because a person needs them for household peace and the benefit from them is greater (Merkevet ha-Mishneh, Shabbat 5:8; and see further explanations in Aruch ha-Shulchan 104:3).

as it is said, “the charge of My terumot,” etc.. The Sages learned from this verse that one may not benefit from tevel because part of it is destined to become terumah. And from the plural word “terumot” they learned that just as it is forbidden to benefit from pure tevel, so too it is forbidden to benefit from impure tevel and burn it, even though the terumah that will be separated from this tevel is destined to be burned (see Hilchot Terumot 2:14).
they do not cover tevel with earth. They do not cover seeds of tevel with soil so that they will sprout.
even produce whose processing was not completed. And which is not yet tevel, nevertheless one must separate from it before sowing it again.
for he has not yet gathered the produce. For the produce is still attached to the plant.
to add to their own bulk. That they themselves will continue to grow, like seedlings with fruit.
that they harden and the seed takes from them. That they harden and another crop grows from them.
it is forbidden. To replant them before separating from them.
because it is like sowing wheat or barley of tevel. As explained in the previous paragraph.
a litra of tevel ma'aser which he sowed and it improved, and it is now ten litras. He sowed a litra of first tithe from which terumat ma'aser had not been separated, and ten litras grew.
is obligated in tithing. Although he must separate terumot and ma'aserot from the crop that grew, the Sages obligated him to separate terumat ma'aser also for the litra that he sowed.

and for that litra he tithes from another place by calculation. For the litra he sowed he must separate from other first-tithe produce that is obligated in terumat ma'aser; he cannot separate from the produce that grew from the litra, since it is not tithe but ordinary produce.
that he rectified it. He separated terumot and ma'aserot from it.
he does not tithe by calculation of the increase, etc.. He must separate again for the onions that he sowed, and not only for what was added to them (the reason is explained in the next halakhah).
edible seeds. That are fit for eating.
and he smoothed them. He finished their processing (see above 3:13).
and their seed does not perish. These seeds do not rot in the ground but remain in it after being sown.

it is in doubt whether they are obligated in tithes rabbinically. It is doubtful whether he must separate only for the increase or whether the Sages obligated him to separate also for the original seed, even though he already separated from it.
and these are not like onions. For which separating again is required without doubt, as stated in the previous halakhah.

for onions are not normally sown. Several later authorities wrote, based on the Gemara (Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 70a), that the Rambam's text should be emended to read “and onions are normally sown.” Because of this, onions that were sown are nullified relative to the crops that grew from them, and if he wants to pull up the onions he sowed and eat them, he must tithe them again. But seeds that reached the one-third stage are not normally sown, so there is doubt about whether they require separating again (see Yeshuot Malko, Aruch ha-Shulchan 104:15-16; and see Rabbi Kafih and others who reconciled the text we have).
three threshing floors. Three crops.
that is in it. That are contained in the tevel he sowed; and since the seed did not perish, they were stringent about its produce.

one does not sell tevel, etc.. One should not sell tevel unless he needs to, and he should sell only to a chaver, that is, a Torah scholar about whom there is no concern that he will eat from it before separating (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 5:8).
and it is forbidden to send the tevel. As a gift.
he must take out their tithes from other produce. To separate for them from other tevel produce.

they compel the seller to rectify; it is a fine on him for having sold the tevel. And even if we know that the seller said at the time of the sale that the produce was tevel, the obligation to separate is nevertheless on him because he sold tevel (Radbaz).
because it is like selling it. For he is giving the tevel in exchange for the loan he made to him, which is like a sale.
if it is because of a debt he owes them, he must take out tithes for them. One who repays his debt with tevel must rectify it and separate tithes from it.
and the buyer. The purchaser.
tithes from this for that. For one must assume that it is all the same year's crop (see Hilchot Terumot 5:11, that one may not separate from the produce of one year for the produce of another year).
one who takes a field on terms. To work it in return for a certain percentage of the crop.
divides. The crop, in order to give the field's owner his share.
and gives to the field's owner. And he is not obligated to separate for him, since they are partners in the crop.
so that he knows that he took tevel. And an Israelite will not err and eat from it without separation (see Radbaz).
but one who leases a field from an Israelite. To work it in return for a fixed quantity of produce regardless of the quantity the field yields.

if he gave him from the seed of that field, he separates terumah, etc.. The lessee must separate terumah gedolah, since terumah gedolah must be separated from the crop before it is taken from the threshing floor. But the separation of the tithes he can leave to the lessor (commentators, based on the Jerusalem Talmud, Ma'aserot 3:1).
and if he gave him from the seed of another field or of another kind, etc.. In which case it is like paying a debt, so he must also separate tithes before giving it to him.
fallow. Not cultivated.
until he needs to and sells it to an Israelite. So that he will reach the point of selling it to an Israelite; this refers to a field in the Land of Israel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 6:2).
one who takes his ancestors' field from a gentile. The Israelite's ancestral field is now owned by the gentile, and the Israelite takes it from him to work it.

they fined him, etc.. In leasing they fined him even when it is not his ancestral field, as stated at the beginning of the halakhah. The commentators on the Rambam gave several explanations for this distinction (see Radbaz and Aruch ha-Shulchan 105:10, 105:14).
who is a lessee, etc.. See also Hilchot Sechirut 8:1-2.
one can say to his fellow. While the produce is still tevel.
he should not say to him, “You take wheat and I barley,” etc.. For he gives him his share of the wheat in exchange for his fellow's share of the barley, and this is like a sale (see also below 11:6).
in order to nullify the gifts due to their brothers the priests. To take the gifts for themselves.
the terumah or the tithe is theirs. For presumably they sold with the understanding that these would be theirs.

and if they sold after the processing was completed, the terumah and the tithe belong to the buyer. Since they could have separated and taken what they separated, yet they sold the produce, it is reasonable that they intended to sell the right to the tithes as well.
who took a field. To work it, in return for part of the crop.
just as they divide the ordinary produce, so they divide the terumah and the tithes. When they divide the crop as agreed, they divide the terumah and the tithes in the same proportion.
the terumah. If the field's owner is a priest.
or the tithe. First tithe, if the field's owner is a Levite.
and the other gifts they divide. For example, second tithe, which is not designated for a Levite or a priest and both may eat it in Jerusalem, so neither has priority regarding it.
one who takes olives to extract oil from them. And the separation is done only after the oil is produced (above 3:15).

just as they divide the ordinary produce, so they divide the terumah and the tithes. And even an Israelite who took from a priest or Levite does not give them all the terumah or the tithe (contrary to the rule explained in the previous halakhah).
because oil is important. And the one who took does not forgo his share of the terumah or tithe.

he is considered to have reserved the place of the tithe. This should be explained as meaning that he reserved a certain right in the field itself with respect to the produce; for if he reserved nothing in the field itself but only a right in the future produce, he does not acquire it when it grows, since one cannot acquire something that has not yet come into the world (see Hilchot Mechirah 23:4).

and if the priest died, his son is like the other priests. Since he did not explicitly reserve for his son too, we explain that he reserved only for himself, and after his death his son has no priority over the other priests.
he sold it to another, etc.. If the buyer sold the field and it is no longer before him, the priest lost his right, and it does not return even if the buyer bought the field again.
an Israelite who took a field from a priest and a Levite. And must give the terumah or the tithe to the field's owner, as above, halakhah 17.
and said. The Israelite.
on condition that the tithes are mine. That he may give them to whichever priest or Levite he wishes.
for a priest does not make a priest. Since he gives the Israelite the right to the terumot and tithes without time limit, it is as though he made him a priest.
who owed a debt to an Israelite. Who was indebted to an Israelite.

this Israelite should not collect from others and separate until he is repaid against his debt. He should not collect tevel from others and separate the tithe for himself up to the amount of the debt.
for this Levite does not make his creditor like another Levite. For he takes the tithes on a regular basis.
smoothed tevel. After smoothing, when it is obligated in separation.
from his mother's father, a priest. For his mother's father acquired the terumah, and likewise the tithe (see above 1:4, that first tithe is not taken from a priest's hand).

and that mother's father inherited from his own mother's father, an Israelite. For although the tevel originally belonged to the Israelite, after the Israelite's death the priest who inherited acquired the terumah and the tithe.

and they are his. The Israelite who inherits from his mother's father the priest receives from him his rights in the tevel, so the terumah and the tithe belong to him, and since he cannot eat the terumah he sells it to a priest (Rikevo and Radbaz).
for the gifts that are fit to be separated. For example, smoothed tevel from which one can separate.
as if they had been separated. We treat them as though they had already been separated, and therefore his mother's father the priest acquired them.
even though they have not yet been separated. See also Hilchot Ishut 5:6.
even though they had not yet reached the time for tithes. Even though he gave the field before the crop reached the stage of growth at which the obligation of tithes begins (see above 2:3-5).

he must tithe on their behalf. When the crop reaches the stage of separation, he must separate also for their share of the crop (some explain that regarding one who gave to a gentile the reason is a fine for having given him a field in the Land of Israel, and regarding one who is not trusted with tithes the reason is so as not to cause him to stumble by eating tevel; Chazon Ish, Demai 14:2, and see above 2:6 and the other commentators there).
he does not need to tithe on their behalf. For most ignoramuses do tithe.
and once they reached the time for tithes, he must tithe on their behalf. For if he does not tithe, he is like one selling tevel to an ignoramus (Radbaz).
and he takes. He separates tithes.
and he need not be concerned about what they ate. He need not separate for the tevel produce they may have eaten before he separated.
tevel by Torah law. Obligated in separation by the Torah.
two logs... they are terumah. For the measure of terumah gedolah for an average person is one fiftieth (see Hilchot Terumot 3:2).
and nine are second tithe. For second tithe is a tenth of what remains after separating first tithe (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 6:3).
he should not begin and drink, etc.. It is forbidden to drink on the basis that he will leave the tithes for the end.
and we do not say, etc.. Even though he drinks with the intention of leaving the tithes for the end, one cannot say that what he leaves at the end is considered as already separated from the start.

and we do not say, regarding a Torah obligation, let it be considered as if it were selected. But where the obligation is rabbinic, one can rely on “bererah” (retroactive designation) (see Hilchot Terumot 1:21 and the explanation there, and see below 9:10).
until it is selected. Until it is actually separated.
one who fixes his tithes at the mouth of the barrel. One who says that the wine found in the upper part of the barrel is the tithes for the rest of the barrel.
he should not drink from its bottom. From the liquid near the bottom.
at its bottom. If he fixed the tithes at the bottom of the barrel.
because the liquids are mixed. And he might drink from the tithes.
but one who fixes it at the mouth of the granary, etc.. A granary is a grain storehouse, and with dry food the parts do not mix.
and a person has. He has permission.
and redeems it. Transfers the holiness of the tithe to a coin, and the tithe becomes ordinary produce again.
and again makes it first tithe. If he separated second tithe before first tithe (Rikevo).

or terumat ma'aser for another place. He may designate all of it as terumat ma'aser for a large quantity of other produce that is first tithe and obligated in a large amount of terumat ma'aser (Derech Emunah). But he cannot make it terumah gedolah (see Ra'avad, Rikevo and Kesef Mishneh; and see Yeshuot Malko, who explained this halakhah differently).
one who sets aside produce. He designates produce obligated in tithes to make it the tithe on other produce each time he needs it.
and eats and drinks. From other produce, and separates their tithes from the produce he designated.
until all that produce he set aside becomes tithe. Until the tithes he separated accumulate to the amount of all the produce he designated and all of it has become tithe.
he found them lost. If after some time it became clear to him that they no longer exist, and it is doubtful whether they existed at the time he separated.

he must be concerned about everything he separated, and it is not certainly tithed. One must be concerned about rectifying all the produce for which he separated at a time when the existence of the produce he designated is unknown, so he should rectify it again to resolve the doubt (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 3:8).

that he separates for those coins from their share. They agreed in advance that repayment of their debt would be by the lender separating tithes that must be given to a priest, Levite or poor person, and keeping the tithes for himself against the debt.
how does he separate for them. How does he fulfill the obligation of tithes without actually giving.

or second tithe. So reads most manuscripts and printed editions, but it seems to be a scribal error and should be “or poor man's tithe” (Mishneh la-Melech), and so it is in the Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 7:3, and in several manuscripts here.

and he acquires on their behalf through another. He transfers the produce to them through a third person who acquires the tithes for them; since they are not present, someone who is not the owner must acquire it for them.

they were accustomed to take from him... he need not acquire through another. If he is accustomed to give only to them, the tithes are considered acquired by them from the time of separation (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 3:7).

and he deducts from the loan until his entire debt is repaid. He subtracts from the loan amount the value of the tithes he separated, and likewise the next time he separates tithes, until no debt remains.
and sells the terumah. Since he is forbidden to eat it.
and eats the tithes. For tithes are permitted for any person to eat.

he may calculate at the cheap price and need not be concerned about interest. If the produce became cheaper between the loan and the separation, he may calculate the value of the produce at the time of separation and profit thereby, even though this was not agreed in advance (in an ordinary loan this would be interest; see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 9:5).

and the Sabbatical year does not cancel this debt. This loan is not cancelled at the end of the Sabbatical year, since a loan is cancelled only when it can be collected from the borrower himself, whereas here he may collect only from his tithes and not from the borrower (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 30a).

and if the householder comes to retract, he may retract only if, etc.. The owner of the produce cannot unilaterally retract from the agreement and cannot demand that the other pay his debt, but the borrower can unilaterally retract and return the money.
the owners despaired of them. Of repaying the debt, for example he thought he would have no more tithe produce with which to collect the debt.

for one does not separate for what is lost. For the debt is considered something lost that does not exist, and so the owner of the produce can no longer keep for himself tithes that he separates for repayment of the debt.

until he takes permission from the heirs, and provided that he leaves them land. To continue the agreement he must ensure that the heirs wish to do so, and also that the deceased left behind property fit for collection, so that the loan will not be considered lost.
even as much as a needle's worth. Even if the land is the size of a needle.
but if they left money, the heir's permission does not help. Since a debt is not collected from movable property the heirs inherited (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:7), the debt no longer exists.
and if he lent them in front of a court. To the fathers.
he need not take permission from the heirs. By rabbinic enactment (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 30b).
if the poor man became rich, they do not separate for him. For he is no longer entitled to the poor man's tithe.
and the other acquires what is in his hand. The borrower need not repay the loan, since when this loan cannot be repaid through separating tithes, the lender lost out.

an Israelite who said to a Levite, “You have a kor of tithe with me,” etc.. An Israelite who separated tithe and told a Levite that he is giving it to him: the Levite may rely on him even though he did not perform an act of acquisition.
for another place. For other first-tithe produce.
he has against him only a complaint. The first Levite cannot sue the Israelite but can only be angry with him for not keeping his word.

and he gave a se'ah to the Levite and a se'ah to the poor man. The amount that must be separated from ten se'ah so that eight remain rectified, but he did not specify that the two se'ah he is giving are to rectify particular produce from the storehouse, but gave without specification.

unless he knows that two se'ah of tithes exist. In which case he can designate them as tithes for the eight se'ah he removes from the storehouse, so the tithes are now separated for particular produce. But if the se'ah he gave are not in the possession of the Levite and the poor man, one cannot say that it now becomes clear that he gave them as tithes for the eight se'ah he removed from the storehouse, for we do not say regarding a Torah obligation that it is considered selected until it is selected (above, halakhah 1), and so he lost what he gave.
but according to the calculation of what remains of the two se'ah. For example, if half a se'ah remains with the Levite and half a se'ah with the poor man, he may eat five se'ah from the storehouse.
and they took a se'ah from the threshing floor. Which is still obligated in tithes.
exempt from tithes. For gifts to the poor are exempt (Hilchot Terumot 2:9).

even though it was done with the householder's permission. Even though the householder agreed to exchange for them the se'ah of gifts with another se'ah, nevertheless the se'ah the poor first took is the se'ah of gifts and not the last se'ah.
baskets. Baskets.
whose terumah was taken. And only tithes must be separated from them.
and he said, “the tithes of this one are in that one”. He fixed the tithes of one basket in the produce of the other basket.
the first is tithed, for he fixed its tithes in the second. And at the time of fixing, the first was still obligated in tithes, and one can separate from it for other produce.
and the second is not tithed, for one does not separate, etc.. By the rule that one does not separate from the exempt for the obligated (above 1:6).
for it is still obligated in the tithes of both. For one must take out of it the tithes of the first, and afterward separate from it for the produce remaining in it.
the tithe of each of them is fixed in the other. And he did not put one basket before the other (unlike the previous halakhah).
he named, etc.. And he cannot retract his words and separate for them from other produce.

he takes out the tithes of both, etc.. When the baskets are equal, one should assume that he did not intend specifically to fix the tithe of each in the other but intended to fix the tithes of both together within them, so he may separate from one for both, or from each for itself, or from each for the other. But when they are not equal, one should assume that he intended specifically to fix the tithe of each in the other (Radbaz).

these are called chullin. Although the produce is still forbidden to eat so long as the tithes have not been separated from it (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:20), it is called chullin because the terumot (called holy) were taken out of it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 7:7).
other tithes. First tithe, and also second tithe or poor man's tithe.
rectified chullin. From which everything required was separated and which is permitted to eat.
a kind with its own kind. The tevel and the chullin are of the same kind.

for it is impossible to follow the taste. For if they were of different kinds one could check whether the tevel gave flavor to the chullin, and if not the mixture is permitted (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:6, and see there halakhah 12).
if he has other produce. Which is also obligated in tithes.
takes out, etc.. He separates for the tevel in the mixture from the other produce, and the mixture is permitted.
until he separates. Part of the mixture in order to permit the rest.

the amount of the terumat ma'aser in the tevel. The measure of terumat ma'aser that must be separated from the tevel (and this refers to tevel from which terumah gedolah was separated but terumat ma'aser was not yet separated; see the next halakhah).

a hundred se'ah of tevel mixed with a hundred se'ah of rectified chullin, he separates from all of it a hundred and one, etc.. Since the tevel mixed with the rectified chullin, the mixture must be divided in two. Therefore he takes out of the mixture a hundred se'ah, the quantity of the tevel that mixed in, and these are considered tevel and he separates terumot and tithes from them. In addition he takes from the rectified chullin that remains one more se'ah, the measure of terumat ma'aser, for the reason that will be explained in the next paragraph.
he loses one se'ah. For before they mixed he had a hundred rectified chullin and now only ninety-nine.
and likewise if that tevel was tevel for terumah. If the tevel mixed before he separated terumah gedolah from it.

he loses from the rectified chullin the amount of terumah and terumat ma'aser. He must take out of the mixture a hundred and three se'ah (since the measure of terumah gedolah for an average person is one fiftieth, that is two se'ah out of a hundred).

and why does he lose this se'ah. The usual law is that when a se'ah of terumat ma'aser mixes into a hundred se'ah of chullin, it is nullified in them and does not forbid them, but one must separate from the mixture one se'ah against the terumat ma'aser and give it to a priest (Hilchot Terumot 13:1). In this case, the tevel fell into rectified chullin, and the tevel includes its terumat ma'aser. Admittedly this terumat ma'aser was already nullified in the hundred se'ah of rectified chullin into which it fell; if so, it must be understood why he needs to take out another se'ah from the rectified chullin.

so that he not say, etc.. If he takes out a hundred and leaves a hundred, one could err and think that the hundred he took out are against the chullin and the hundred he left are against the tevel. Therefore he takes out one more se'ah to show that the pile he left is the pile of chullin that needed rectification (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 7:7).
and likewise if the tevel was less, etc.. Even in cases where the produce is not in equal proportion.
he lifts out the tevel. He removes from the mixture the quantity of the tevel.
tevel ma'aser. From which a tenth for terumat ma'aser has not yet been separated.

forbids at any amount. If both are of the same kind, since it can be permitted by separation and it falls under “something that has permitters,” which is not nullified if both are of the same kind (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:9-12).
if he has other tithe. From which he has not separated terumat ma'aser.
he lifts out the tithe that mixed in, etc.. He takes out of the mixture a certain quantity according to the amount of tithe that mixed in, plus a tenth of the tithe.

a hundred of tithe that mixed with a hundred of rectified chullin, he separates from all of it a hundred and ten. A hundred against the tithe that mixed in, and ten more that he loses from the chullin as the measure of terumat ma'aser contained in a hundred se'ah of tithe (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 7:7, where he expanded on the reason for this law).
and whatever he separated is tithe. The hundred and ten he took out have the law of tithe, and he separates from them a tenth for terumat ma'aser (Aruch ha-Shulchan 107:11).
if the tevel exceeded the tithe. For example, a hundred of tevel mixed with ninety of tithe.

for if he names the terumat ma'aser in the tevel, etc.. If he designates a certain se'ah of the mixture as the terumat ma'aser of the tevel and takes it out together with the ninety he takes out against the tithe, that se'ah will forbid the ninety, so they did not require him to take out this se'ah.
mixed (medumma). A mixture of terumah and chullin that has the law of terumah as a whole (terumah is called “dema” in the Torah).

and he separates the tevel and the measure of terumat ma'aser of the tevel and one percent of the tithe. He takes out of the mixture the quantity of the tevel plus the terumat ma'aser of the tevel, and adds one percent of the quantity of the tithe, which has the law of terumat ma'aser.
and the tevel is entirely medumma. Since it contains the measure of its own terumat ma'aser and that of the tithe, and there are not a hundred to nullify them.
and he sells it to the priest. For only he is permitted to eat it.
except for the value of the two terumot in it. Which must be given to the priests free, as the law of terumah.
and it turns out he loses from the tithe one percent of it, etc.. That he takes out of the tithe one percent, similar to the measure of terumat ma'aser from tevel.
the terumat ma'aser of a hundred tevel. One se'ah of terumat ma'aser from the tevel.
and the measure of terumat ma'aser from two hundred of tithe. Another two se'ah of terumat ma'aser from two hundred of tithe.
if the tevel was equal to the tithe. If equal quantities mixed.

he separates a hundred and one, etc.. By strict law it would suffice to take out of the mixture a hundred against the tithe, and they added one more se'ah against the terumat ma'aser in the tevel, so that it be clear that what he takes out is the tithe which drew with it a further portion equal to the measure of terumat ma'aser (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 7:7).
ten rows of ten jars of wine each. Ten jars in each row, a hundred jars in all. The jars are arranged in an equilateral square, so there are four outer rows, which are the sides of the square.

and he fixed one jar from the outer row as tithe for another place, and it is not known which row is the outer one. He designated one jar to be tithe for wine located elsewhere, and said that this jar would be taken from the outer row, and did not intend a particular row of the four outer rows (see Aruch ha-Shulchan 107:16 and others).
