he takes two barrels diagonally. Thus he took from the four outer rows (a “chavit” is a jar).
and mixes the two and separates from them. He mixes them together and takes out of them one barrel as the tithe, so he has separated from all the outer rows.

he fixed it on half of the outer row, etc.. The four outer rows can be divided into eight half-rows, and if he fixed that the tithe jar be taken from the jars in the eight outer half-rows, he fills one jar for the tithe from the four jars at the four corners, for each of these jars is shared by two half-rows, so he has separated from the eight outer half-rows.
he takes one row diagonally. He takes ten jars forming a diagonal line from one corner to the opposite corner, so he took from every possible row, and fills one jar for the tithe from all of them.
he fixed the tithe on one of them, etc.. He fixed that the tithe jar be taken from the hundred jars and did not refer at all to its place.
in the days of Yochanan the High Priest. Apparently Yochanan Hyrcanus I, son of Shimon ben Matityahu the Hasmonean, who ruled until 104 BCE.

for everyone is careful about terumah gedolah and separates it, etc.. Because terumah gedolah carries a death penalty, and a single grain of wheat exempts the whole pile, so separating it involves no loss. Also, because they thought that the obligation of terumat ma'aser, which also carries death, applies only to the Levite after first tithe was separated, but when first tithe is not separated they mistakenly thought there was no obligation to separate terumat ma'aser (Rikevo, citing Rashi, Bekhorot 11b).
trustworthy, qualified people. See below 10:1.
called demai. Many explanations of the word were given, and in the Commentary on the Mishnah (Berakhot 7:1) he wrote that the word is composed of two Aramaic words: “da mai” - “what is this?”.

a capital sin. One who eats produce from which terumah and terumat ma'aser were not separated is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (but one who eats produce from which tithes were not separated receives lashes for eating it and is not liable to death; see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:19-20).
because there is no loss in it. Separating it involves no financial loss to the owners.
its owners eat it. In Jerusalem (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1).

but one does not separate first tithe and poor man's tithe from demai, etc.. Since there is a doubt that the tithes may have been separated properly, the Levite or poor man cannot take the tithes, as with any monetary doubt where one who wants to extract money from his fellow must bring proof (and see the next halakhah and below halakhah 5, that nevertheless one must designate these tithes).
to name it. To define a certain portion of the produce or grain as poor man's tithe.
a tenth of what is here. A tenth of the produce.

in order to establish second tithe, etc.. To strengthen the enactment to separate second tithe from demai, they ordained that poor man's tithe also be designated from it. For in the years in which poor man's tithe is separated (the third and sixth years of the Sabbatical cycle), second tithe is not separated, and people might get used to separating only terumat ma'aser in the other years too, in which second tithe must be separated.
while he is naked. For it is forbidden to recite a blessing while naked, but to separate is permitted (compare Hilchot Terumot 4:4).
and places it beside the produce. So that it will be adjacent to the rest of the tithe.
this is tithe. The one percent he separated is part of the first tithe.
and the rest of the tithe is adjacent to it. Another nine parts of the hundred are adjacent to the part separated (and he does not separate the first tithe but only names it).
this of which I said that it is tithe. The portion actually separated.
for he may not separate terumat ma'aser before the tithe in the first instance. Therefore he first names the first tithe and only afterward separates terumat ma'aser from it.
and it is permitted to separate second tithe before first tithe with demai. But with certain tevel it is forbidden in the first instance to precede second with first (Hilchot Terumot 3:23).
and if he wishes. Not to separate the second tithe but to redeem it immediately with money (for the manner of redemption see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 4:1).
from the baker. Who is not trusted regarding tithes.

the measure of terumat ma'aser and challah. Since ignoramuses are suspected regarding challah, the buyer must separate it (Yeshuot Malko). Others say that ignoramuses were not suspected regarding challah (just as they were not suspected regarding terumah), but the Sages ordained that a baker who is an ignoramus does not separate but only the one who buys from him does (see Radbaz on halakhah 12 below, and Hilchot Bikkurim 8:14).

he has challah and second tithe at its north. Ordinarily one separates terumot and tithes from the grain and only afterward separates challah from the dough. But in this case, where the separation is done after baking, they put the separation of challah before second tithe because Israel became obligated in challah immediately upon entering the Land, whereas they became obligated in tithes only after conquering and settling. First tithe precedes both because the Torah calls it “reshit” (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 5:1, citing the Jerusalem Talmud).
that he may eat at his house. On the Sabbath.
he says on the eve of the Sabbath. Because it is forbidden to separate tithes on the Sabbath and festivals, since it looks like repairing (Hilchot Shabbat 23:9).
but with certain tevel. Produce from which terumot and tithes were certainly not separated.
that is in his possession. In his ownership.
and he is in the study hall or in the field. Close to the onset of the Sabbath.
the two figs that I will separate are terumah. For with certain tevel one must also separate terumah gedolah, whose measure is one fiftieth.
and ten. That is, 9.8 figs, which is approximately ten, since he separates from the remaining 98 figs.
and nine. For he has already separated two for terumah gedolah and ten for first tithe and 88 figs remain, and nine figs are approximately a tenth of that (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 7:4).
to murmur with his lips. To repeat quietly the wording of the separation.

it is permitted to move it on the Sabbath. For there is a way to rectify it for eating (unlike ordinary tevel, which it is forbidden to move because it cannot be eaten on the Sabbath; see Hilchot Shabbat 25:19).

and he looks at one side and eats the rest. He does not actually separate as on a weekday because that looks like repairing, but looks at one side and designates it in his mind for terumah and tithe, and eats the rest (Rash"s, Demai 7:5; Sha'arei Tzedek, Sha'ar Mitzvot ha-Aretz chapter 13; Chochmat Adam 13; Responsa Rav Pe'alim 3, Orach Chaim 25). It may also be explained that the reason he does not actually separate is that it is forbidden to move the first tithe, since it is forbidden to eat so long as the Levite has not separated terumat ma'aser from it (see Pesikta Rabbati section 25).
at the bottom of the cup. At the base of the cup.
at the mouth of the cup. In its upper part.
a worker who does not trust the householder. And the householder supplies his food.
a dried fig. A dried fig.

and second tithe is the last ten. That is, nine dried figs, approximately ten, since after he called ten by the name first tithe, ninety dried figs remain, from which he must separate second tithe (Tosafot Anshei Shem, Demai 7:3).

for it is a condition of the court that terumat ma'aser be from the householder's and second tithe from the worker's. It is a rabbinic enactment that terumat ma'aser is at the householder's expense and second tithe at the worker's expense. Therefore if it was agreed that the worker would eat a hundred dried figs and the worker separated one of them for terumat ma'aser, the worker may eat another dried fig at the householder's expense, but the worker redeems the second tithe with his own money.
the bakers. Who are careful about tithes and purity and who used demai flour.

they did not obligate them to separate second tithe from demai. They were lenient with them because they are required to sell at a price set by the market inspectors and do not have large profits (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 2:4, based on Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 9a).

so that he separates it in purity together with the challah. For if he sells to someone who is not careful about purity, the terumat ma'aser would become impure (based on the Gra, Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 2:4). Some explain that even if the buyer is careful about purity, they obligated the baker to separate because it is easier to be careful about the purity of the terumah when it is separated immediately (Chazon Yechezkel, Demai 3:13).
the retailer. A person who buys from the baker and sells to others.

must separate even second tithe. Because there are no inspectors forcing a seller to the retailer to sell at a low price (Aruch ha-Shulchan 109:11; Pe'at ha-Shulchan, Demai 14:12, note 38). Others explain that because children also buy from the retailer, they might buy from the baker too and eat the bread before separating second tithe (Yad Peshutah).
even though this trustworthy person tithed his share. The one trusted with tithes tithed his share when he harvested the grapes before bringing them into the winepress.

he must still separate from it demai tithes for half the ignoramus's share. Because in the winepress the wine from the tithed grapes mixed with the wine from the ignoramus's grapes. When the wine is later divided, each portion turns out to be half from tithed grapes and half from demai grapes.
they were half and half. If half the grapes belonged to the one trusted with tithes and half to the one not trusted.
and ten for second tithe. That is, nine logs, approximately ten (see above, halakhah 11).
he separates by calculation. For example, if fifty were his and a hundred and fifty were from the one not trusted, he separates a log and a half for terumat ma'aser and fifteen logs for second tithe.
what he eats. Whether his own or the ignoramus's.
and what he sells. His own.
and what he buys. He buys from an ignoramus in order to sell (Radbaz).

and he does not accept hospitality at an ignoramus's house. On his own initiative (and if he must accept hospitality, he separates from what he eats as explained above, 9:7, and below halakhot 6-7; Aruch ha-Shulchan 110:1).
in public. In front of three people.
is believed forever. And need not accept it in front of three (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 2:3).
and the members of his household. People who live in the house on a regular basis, such as a servant or an adopted son (Derech Emunah).
even if he brought them in that very day. Who died on the very day he brought the produce into his house.
they are presumed rectified. For it is presumed that a chaver does not let anything unrectified leave his hands (Rikevo).
his wife. Who was widowed or divorced.
in the first instance. At the time of the marriage or the sale.
until they are suspected. Until it is discovered that they are not trustworthy.
accustomed. Accustomed to being in his house.

must accept. Because they have been accustomed to an ignoramus from a young age, there is concern they were influenced by him. But the wife and daughter of a chaver who married an ignoramus, or a grown slave of a chaver who was sold to an ignoramus, are already accustomed to behaving as chaverim (Yad Peshutah).
and one of his sons or slaves was trusted. Who accepted upon himself to be trusted.
they buy from him. From the father.
and eat on their word. On the word of the trusted slave or son, when they testify that the produce is rectified.
if he was trusted and his wife was not trusted, they buy from him. For he certainly tithed what he sells.
but they do not accept hospitality from him. For his wife is suspected of serving food that is not rectified.
and a curse will come. An expression of a curse.
he should not serve. He should not work as a waiter.
unless everything under his hand is tithed and rectified. For it is forbidden to serve demai to others, since he causes them to stumble in a prohibition.
they saw him reclining. Participating in the meal.
the meal is not presumed tithed. For the chaver is not obligated to rectify the food served to the other diners.
perhaps the chaver relies on the stipulations in his heart. Perhaps the chaver stipulated before the meal to separate tithes from what he will eat at the meal (see above 9:7-11).
even if he was with him at the drinking. At the same meal. For a chaver bears no responsibility for what an ignoramus eats.
a fine loaf. Skillfully made seasoned bread (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 6:12).
he buys for him without specification and is exempt from tithing. For he is merely the ignoramus's agent.
and if he exchanged the ma'ah. He bought with his own money and took in exchange the ignoramus's coin.
he must tithe. For then it is as if he sold the demai to the ignoramus, and he must tithe what he sells (above, halakhah 1).
and if the chaver specified, etc.. In the case where he exchanged the ma'ah.

and this which he bought for his fellow, he need not tithe. Since he told the seller that this bunch was for the ignoramus, the seller transfers it directly to the ignoramus through him, and the chaver is not considered to be selling demai himself but an agent (Rabbi Kafih).

and if they were mixed... he rectifies everything as demai. Lest he give the ignoramus the bunch he took for himself, which he is already obligated to tithe (and the bunch is not nullified by majority, because the mixture can be rectified and permitted to eat by separating tithes from it, and something with permitters is not nullified; Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:10).
and brought to each one separately. He gave each of the five his own portion by itself.
the chaverim among them need tithe only their own portion. For they have no responsibility for the ignoramuses' portions.
he brought it to them mixed. He brought them all the bunches of vegetables together, such that each must take his portion himself.

the chaverim among them must tithe everything. For if they divide the vegetables among themselves it is as if the chaver gives from his own to the ignoramus, and it is forbidden for a chaver to give his own demai to an ignoramus unless he has tithed it (Kesef Mishneh).
go and gather for me. Gather for me.
the chaver may eat from them casually. A casual meal, and he does not separate terumot and tithes that have not yet been fixed for tithing (above 3:1, 5:5-6).

and tithes them as demai. If he wants to eat from them as a fixed meal, he tithes them as demai, like one accepting hospitality from an ignoramus. Because he gathered the produce for the ignoramus, and ignoramuses are careful about terumah gedolah, we assume that the ignoramus separated terumah gedolah for it from elsewhere (Radbaz, and see Tosefta ki-Fshutah, Ma'aserot p. 680).

even though chaverim were not suspected of separating terumah from other than adjacent produce. For it is forbidden in the first instance to separate terumah from produce that is not adjacent to one another (Hilchot Terumot 3:17-20).

to remove the stumbling block from before the ignoramus, they separate. For after the fact the terumah takes effect (ibid.). And it is better to separate in this way to save the ignoramus from eating tevel (Tosefta Ma'aserot 2:5; Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 32a).

it is permitted to feed, etc.. They permitted the poor and guests to eat demai in order to ease matters for charity-givers and hosts, so that they could use demai for charity and hospitality (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 3:1).
and one must inform them. That they were given demai, so that if they wish to be stringent they can rectify the produce themselves.

they collect without specification from everyone. They do not collect separately from ignoramuses for poor ignoramuses and from chaverim for poor chaverim, because if they collected separately, the ignoramuses would be offended and give less charity (Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 3:1).
and if the demai belonged to a doctor, he may not give even into his hand. For a chaver does not feed anything unrectified (Kesef Mishneh).
to send him. As a gift.
those who give generous measure. Sellers who sell in abundance, measuring the merchandise in large measuring vessels (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 2:4).
the wholesalers. A merchant who buys from many people and sells in large measure (ibid., and see below 14:1).
because they add to the measure. And the buyer receives more than he is owed. Therefore they ordained that the buyer separate the gifts.
in small measure. Small measuring vessels.
profits. Earns.
he should send. As a gift. Although he does not profit from a gift, the Sages did not distinguish in this (Rambam la-Am).
half a se'ah. About four litras.
a dinar. A silver coin weighing 96 barleycorns (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 2:5).

by estimate. By approximation, without weighing or counting. Although this manner resembles selling in large measure, they did not permit selling demai this way, because they exempted from separating demai only one who adds to the measure, but one who sells by estimate does not add to the measure (Perush Tevunah on Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 2:5).

one of them said, etc.. If he sold in small measure and the buyer wanted to separate even though the obligation is on the seller, or he sold in large measure and the seller wanted to separate even though the obligation is on the buyer (Merkevet ha-Mishneh, Rash"s on Demai 2:5).
and this is a condition of the court. Compare above 9:11.
who inherited from their father, an ignoramus. They inherited from him produce presumed to be demai.
you take the wheat in such-and-such place and I the wheat in such-and-such place. Each of them has a share in the wheat and each is considered to be receiving his own share.
because this one is selling demai. For it is like exchanging his share of the wheat for his brother's share of the barley (see also above 6:14).
vegetables. Already bundled and fixed for tithing (Rikevo, Radbaz).
as demai. Without separating terumot and tithes.

one who buys vegetables from the market. And has already agreed with the seller on the price per bundle of vegetables, and all that remains is to count how many bundles he took (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 3:2, based on the Jerusalem Talmud).
and pulled. He lifted the vegetables and thereby performed an act of acquisition, and by law he cannot retract (see Hilchot Mechirah 3:4).
and decided to return them to the shopkeeper. He regretted it and decided to return the vegetables, and the seller agrees.
he should not return until he tithes. For by law he acquired the vegetables and consequently became obligated to tithe them.

if most bring them into their houses, he is exempt from tithing. For the produce is not yet fixed for tithing, and one may eat from it casually until he brings it into his house (above 3:1-2). We assume that produce that fell on the road has not yet entered a house, so he is exempt from tithing if he eats from it on the road.
and if most bring them in to sell in the market. In which case they were fixed for tithing once their processing was completed (above 3:1).
these are demai. For they were already obligated in tithes even if they did not enter a house, and out of concern that the owners did not tithe the produce properly, he must tithe it immediately.
he took them to eat them. The produce he found on the road.
and decided to put them away. To keep them to eat later.
and if he took them at first so they would not be lost. So that they would not lie there in disgrace, and not in order to eat them.
these are permitted, etc.. Since he did not intend to acquire them, he is not responsible for any stumbling that might come from them (Rikevo).
until he wishes to eat them... he tithes them. And then he acquires them and must tithe.
the trimmings of vegetables. The spoiled tips cut off from the vegetable.
found in the garden. And we assume the gardener cut them off, and they are not fit for eating (see Hilchot Terumot 11:10).
they are exempt from demai. For there is no obligation to separate terumot and tithes except from something fit to eat.
found in the house they are obligated. For some householders are more particular about their food and cut off from the vegetable even parts still fit to eat (Radbaz).
on a trash heap, everywhere it is permitted. For what is thrown on the trash is no longer considered food.
to the innkeeper. The innkeeper (a woman); it is the custom of merchants to give her flour and meat and she cooks and bakes for them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 3:5).
he tithes what he gives her. So that if she or others eat from his, they will not stumble in a prohibition.
and tithes what he takes from her. Lest she gave him from her own or from others' who do not tithe.

because she is suspected of switching. Because many guests are with her it is common for her to become confused and switch their food (Aruch ha-Shulchan, Yoreh De'ah 119:17). Some explain that because the innkeeper toils for the guest, she permits herself to take the guest's good food for herself and give him in its place her own inferior food (Tosafot, Chullin 6b; Pe'at ha-Shulchan, Demai 16:13, note 22; Aruch ha-Shulchan 111:20).
to his mother-in-law. Even though she is the wife of an ignoramus who is not trusted regarding tithes.
he need not be concerned about tithes. That she may have given him food that is not tithed.
nor about the Sabbatical year. That she may have given him Sabbatical-year aftergrowth, which is forbidden to eat (see Hilchot Shemitah 4:2-3).

because she is not suspected of switching. For ignoramuses in general are not suspected of switching something deposited with them (Aruch ha-Shulchan, Yoreh De'ah 119:17). Or because it is the way of neighbors to toil for one another, so a neighbor does not permit herself to switch the foods (Tosafot, ibid.); and the law of his mother-in-law is like that of his neighbor (Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 3:6), because she is not suspected of feeding her daughter forbidden food (Radbaz).
when he gave her leaven for the dough and spices for the pot. And she has everything she needs for the cooking or baking.
but if he did not give, he is concerned about tithes. Lest she added spices or used leaven from demai.
to a grinder. A miller.
perhaps he switched them with an ignoramus's wheat. For many people, including ignoramuses, bring him wheat to grind.
uses a chaver's shop. Acts as seller or as waiter serving food to the people who come to dine there (see Tosefta ki-Fshutah, Demai p. 226).
even though the chaver goes in and out. Of the shop, and there are times when the ignoramus is there alone.
they are like the produce of a gentile, who is presumed to switch a deposit. And they are not like demai produce, for an ordinary gentile has no produce of others except a miller, as above (Rikevo).
whose processing was not yet completed. For example, grain that was reaped and threshed but not yet winnowed or smoothed (above 3:1).

he separates tithes as we have explained. In Hilchot Terumot 1:11, that produce whose processing was completed in an Israelite's hands is obligated in terumot and tithes even if it grew in a gentile's land.
and if the produce he deposited was tevel and its processing was completed. With an Israelite before he deposited it, and he received back from the gentile produce whose processing was completed.
he must separate, lest the gentile did not switch. But gave him the same tevel produce he deposited with him.

and therefore it seems to me that the tithes he separates are doubtful. For it is possible that the gentile switched and gave him produce that grew in his possession and was processed by him, which is exempt from tithes.

but if he deposited rectified chullin, he need not separate anything. For if the gentile returned the same produce, it was already rectified; and if he switched it, its processing was completed in the gentile's hands and it is exempt from tithes.
as we have explained in Hilchot Terumah. 1:11, that produce that grew in a gentile's possession and had its processing completed by him is exempt from terumot and tithes.

for he cannot tithe. For it is forbidden to separate terumot and tithes on the Sabbath, as it is like repairing his produce (Hilchot Shabbat 23:9, and see another reason there, halakhah 14). And he cannot stipulate (as explained above, 9:7), because the Sabbath has already begun.
and likewise if one who is not trusted said to him. Another ignoramus.
they are tithed. That he knows the produce is tithed.

because the awe of the Sabbath is upon ignoramuses, and he does not commit a transgression through it. For it is serious in their eyes to transgress and to lie on the Sabbath (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 4:1).
until he tithes with demai tithing. That he tithe according to the law of demai (above 9:2).
for having eaten on the Sabbath. Although he cannot retroactively rectify the produce he ate, he separates for it on account of the robbery of the priests (Tosefta ki-Fshutah, Demai p. 245).
and for the remainder. Which he must rectify from now on. For they permitted relying on the ignoramus only for the needs of the Sabbath.
because it did not seem right to tithe in the meantime. For it is impossible to tithe either on the Sabbath or on a festival, so they permitted relying on the ignoramus until he can tithe.
and likewise on the two festival days of the Diaspora. For those outside the Land of Israel add a day to each festival (Hilchot Yom Tov 1:21, Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 5:4-6).

one who vowed concerning his fellow that he would eat with him on the Sabbath. An ignoramus who vowed that if the chaver did not come as his guest on the Sabbath, he would not eat at the chaver's house (Rikevo). And the chaver cannot separate conditionally, since the Sabbath has already begun.

he asks him and eats on his word. A chaver is permitted to be a guest at an ignoramus's house if the ignoramus says the produce is tithed. And although a chaver does not accept hospitality from an ignoramus (above 10:1), here they were lenient because of animosity.
but on the second Sabbath... he should not eat. Without conditions, but should stipulate before the Sabbath, since he already knows the ignoramus wants him to eat at his house.

and we saw that it fell back before us, either in its place or in another place. That the terumat ma'aser fell onto the produce from which it was separated or onto other produce, and if they mix, the mixture would be forbidden to eat (Hilchot Terumot 13:2).

and he said, “I went back and separated it”. That he removed the terumat ma'aser from the produce (Rikevo). Some explain that this refers to a case where the terumat ma'aser mixed with produce in an amount more than a hundred times its own, where the law is that the mixture is permitted to eat but one must separate produce equal to the terumah and give it to a priest; and the ignoramus is believed to say he already did so (Aruch ha-Shulchan 112:13, based on the Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 4:1).

and they are not suspected of feeding a mixture of terumah. A mixture containing terumah. Although they are not careful to separate terumat ma'aser, after it has been separated they are careful with it as with terumah gedolah.
and one trusted regarding second tithe is not trusted regarding first. For perhaps he separates only second tithe, which the owners eat, but not first tithe, which the owners must give to the Levite.
for he redeems all of them. Even the terumat ma'aser he separated, in case all the produce is second tithe, as the ignoramus said (Rikevo).
buy for me. Buy produce for me.
from one who tithes. And he did not ask him to buy from a particular person.
and he went and bought and brought it to him, he is not believed. For there is concern that he bought from one who does not tithe.
buy for me from so-and-so. That he mentioned the name of a particular person who is trusted.
for he fears that he may ask him. That the sender might ask the seller whether the agent bought from him, and it would be discovered that he lied.

and he goes and buys from that so-and-so, even though he does not know him, and eats on his word. For we are not concerned that a person would lie on behalf of another when he himself derives no benefit from it. They were lenient with a guest because he is a stranger and does not know the townspeople (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 4:6).
who here sells old. Old grain, which is better than new (Rash"s, Demai 4:6). Some explain it means grain from the previous year, which has no chadash prohibition (Rav Ovadiah of Bartenura, ibid.).
as if repaying one another. It looks as though they are doing each other a favor.
these are believed. There is no concern that they colluded.
if he knows a person there. Who is his friend and on whom he relies.
he should buy only from the expert. About whom his friend testifies that he is an expert (Merkevet ha-Mishneh).

and if he stayed there thirty days... he should buy only from the expert. That many testify about him that he is an expert (Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that after thirty days he can already know who behaves as a chaver, so he should not rely on others (Derech Emunah, citing Chazon Ish; and see Merkevet ha-Mishneh).
except with terumot and tithes. Because most ignoramuses do tithe.
the donkey-drivers. Merchants who travel from city to city transporting their goods on a donkey.
he is not believed, lest they are colluding with one another. That one testifies for him here so that the other will testify for him in another city.

and the profit will be shared between them. And they will divide the profits (and above, halakhah 7, they were not concerned about reciprocal favors, because there the witnesses are doing each other a favor; but when donkey-drivers come together to a city, there is reasonable suspicion that the business is shared by the two drivers and their testimony is directly for their own benefit; Yad Peshutah).

one who sells produce in Syria. Where produce is obligated in terumot and tithes only rabbinically (see Hilchot Terumot 1:3), and one who buys produce in general from an ignoramus there is not obligated to tithe it, because most is from gentiles (Ra'avad).
it is from the Land of Israel. And produce of the Land of Israel is subject to demai.
they are rectified and tithed. He said the produce is from the Land of Israel but that he rectified it and separated tithes from it.
for the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. Just as the reason to forbid the produce is that we rely on the seller's words, so we may rely on him to permit it.
they are mine. From his own field in Syria, which is obligated in tithes rabbinically.

and if it is known that he has land in Syria and most of his sales are from his field, the buyer from him must tithe, for it is presumed that he brought from his field. Since the produce is obligated in tithes even if the seller had said nothing, the rule that the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted does not apply, and we do not rely on his statement that he tithed.
it is from leket, shichechah and pe'ah. And is exempt from tithes (Hilchot Terumot 2:9).
these are believed. Because most of their livelihood is from gifts to the poor, one should assume that what they have is from those gifts.
the time of the threshing floors. The harvest season.

provided that he is near the threshing floor, so that he can go out and return in a day. Within one day's walking distance of the threshing floor. For if he is farther, there is concern that he already ate the gifts to the poor he gleaned yesterday (Derech Emunah).
the entire year. In a year of poor man's tithe (Rikevo). Because poor man's tithe is given in larger quantity and has no fixed time of giving, it is found all year (Kol Ramaz, Pe'ah 8:2).
this flour is from wheat of leket, shichechah and pe'ah, they are not believed. For people's practice is to give whole wheat to those gleaning leket, shichechah and pe'ah, not flour.
the barley of rice. Rice ears.
groats. Ground, hulled beans.
are believed regarding oil, to say it is poor man's tithe. For it is people's practice to separate poor man's tithe from oil.
nikuf olives. Olives left after the picking, which the poor gather and which are exempt from terumot and tithes (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 8:3, Challah 6:9).
regarding raw vegetables. To say that it is from poor man's tithe (since vegetables have no leket, shichechah and pe'ah).

for it is the custom of householders to give the poor man a little cooked vegetable from his pot. Sometimes the householder forgets to tithe the vegetable while raw and tithes from the cooked vegetable from the pot (Rash"s and other commentators, Pe'ah 8:4). One explains that when the tithe is small the poor man does not wish to bother with it and cook it, so the householder cooks all the vegetables with the tithe in them and then gives it to the poor man cooked (Melechet Shlomo, there, citing Rabbi Yehudah Ashkenazi).
always. In all years, for first tithe applies in all of them.
just as an Israelite is believed regarding terumah gedolah. Above 9:1.

but he is not believed regarding it to exempt it from second tithe. If a chaver bought grain from an ignoramus Levite, the Levite is not believed to say that he separated second tithe from it, even if they saw that he separated first tithe from it (Rikevo). He is not believed like an Israelite who separated first tithe (above, halakhah 5), because the Israelite loses money by giving first tithe to the Levite, and therefore he is believed regarding second tithe; but the Levite gives the first tithe to himself and loses nothing (Derech Emunah, Yad Peshutah).
but one who is suspected of selling terumah as chullin. Selling terumah and saying it is chullin. And he does so because terumah is cheaper and he wants to profit.
something that has a presumption of terumah and tithe. Something in which plant products obligated in terumot and tithes may be mixed.
even fish innards. Even the internal organs of fish, which are not subject to terumot and tithes, are forbidden, lest he mixed in terumah oil.
and only what is before him is forbidden. Of what he sells in the house or in the shop.
but his storehouse. A warehouse or other place where the merchandise is stored.

lest the matter become known and he lose everything. That it becomes known that he mixed terumah into his storehouse, and the whole storehouse would be ostracized (Commentary on the Mishnah, Avodah Zarah 2:7, based on the Babylonian Talmud).
presumption of tithe. Second tithe, which is forbidden to eat outside Jerusalem.
a rabbinic fine. From the words of the Sages.
a suspect who testified about others'. That their produce is rectified.
the presumption is that a person does not sin when he has no benefit. A person does not sin when it is of no use to him, so there is no concern that he lies on behalf of others.
even regarding his own he is believed. Because he is not testifying that the produce is rectified and he has no benefit from it.
provided that he does not appear to be colluding, as we have explained. Above, halakhah 10.
the meat was the meat of a firstborn. A firstborn animal that is forbidden to slaughter until a blemish falls on it, and if one slaughtered it, it is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Bekhorot 3:4).
the wine was libation wine. Wine that was poured as a libation for idolatry, which is forbidden to drink and for benefit.
the strict law is that he is not believed. For a person is not believed to forbid something that is not under his control.
even if the seller was an ignoramus. Whose trustworthiness is less than that of a chaver.
shitin. Wild figs.
and rimin. Wild jujube.
and uzrarin. A bright fruit resembling a small apple that grows on the thorny azarole shrub.

and bnot shuach. A kind of white fig that bears fruit once in three years (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 1:1). Some identify bnot shuach with the stone pine (a type of pine), whose cone seeds are called pine nuts and are edible.
and bnot shikmah. The sycamore tree was used mainly for producing beams from its branches, and its fruits resemble figs but are of poor quality.
and the gufnan. Sumac.

and the nevelot of the date palm, which are those that have not yet formed “leaven”. Dates that fell from the tree before ripening and softening, like dough that swells and softens through leaven (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 1:2).
and the caper. The caper bush.
and the kusbar. Wild coriander.
because their presumption is from ownerless produce. And ownerless produce is exempt from terumot and tithes (Hilchot Terumot 2:11).
even if an ignoramus said to him they are not tithed, they are exempt. Even if it is certain that the produce is not tithed, it is exempt, because its presumption is that it is ownerless (Rikevo).
until it becomes known to him that they are from guarded produce. That they did not grow ownerless, in which case they are obligated in tithes.
the early fruits. The fruits that ripen first.
and the late fruits. Those that ripen last.
all the fruits that ripened early before they set a guard. The first fruits to ripen, so long as they are so few that they are not yet worth the guard's wages and their owners abandon them.
the drying mats. The mats on which figs are dried (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 8:4).
and leave them without a guard. For they are not worth the guard's wages and are ownerless.

and likewise vinegar made from dates is exempt from demai. For the practice is to make vinegar from ownerless dates (Rabbi Kafih). Some read “made from temed”; temed is a fermented drink made from grape waste (pits and skins) and is exempt from tithes because wine waste is ownerless (Kesef Mishneh, based on the Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 1:1).

they decreed only on the produce of the land that those returning from Babylon took possession of. The Land of Israel was sanctified when those who came up from Egypt conquered it, but this sanctity lapsed with the exile. When those returning from Babylon came back to the Land in Ezra's days, they took possession of a smaller area of the Land and sanctified it with a lasting sanctity, which is the determining one for commandments dependent on the Land. Nevertheless, the Sages ordained that some commandments be observed also in the territory of those who came up from Egypt, and they established there, among other things, the separation of terumot and tithes (Hilchot Terumot 1:5). Here it is explained that the Sages did not institute the law of demai in this territory of those who came up from Egypt.
which is from Kezib. A place on the seacoast north of Acre (today called Achziv, about 5 km north of Nahariya).
and inward. Toward the southeast (see Hilchot Terumot 1:7).
and Kezib itself is like the outside. It is considered outside the territory of those who returned from Babylon.

for their presumption is from produce of the place where they were found. And we are not concerned that they were brought from elsewhere. For in the Land of Israel, produce in general is obligated in tithes until it becomes known that it is exempt, and outside the Land, produce in general is exempt until it becomes known that it is obligated. And they treated the land held by those who came up from Egypt as outside the Land with respect to demai (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 1:3).
in Syria. Where produce is obligated in terumot and tithes by rabbinic law (Hilchot Terumot 1:3; and see above 12:11).
the pressed fig cake. A lump of crushed, pressed-together figs.
and large, even carobs. Straight ones, without dents or bulges (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 2:1 and Jerusalem Talmud there).
and large cumin. Whose seeds have a straight shape, unlike Cyprian cumin, whose seeds are rounded (Jerusalem Talmud, ibid.).
in all of the Land of Israel. Even in places held only by those who came up from Egypt.
the donkey-drivers. A caravan of merchants bringing merchandise on donkeys.
to Tyre. Which is within the territory of those who came up from Egypt.
unless it was recognizable. That it is very white, in which case it is evident that it is from the Land of Israel and is subject to demai.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 4.
from storehouse owners. Owners of warehouses.

and we do not say, “perhaps they stored from the produce of the Land”. For donkey-drivers usually bring merchandise from far away to profit more, but storehouse owners usually store from the nearby place (Radbaz).
and likewise a single donkey-driver... is exempt from demai. For it is not the way of a single donkey-driver to bring from a distant place, since he travels alone without a caravan.

in Sidon is obligated in demai because it is closer than Tyre. The Rambam's words are difficult, since Tyre is farther south than Sidon and closer to the Land of Israel. In the Tosefta (Demai 1:10) it is indeed stated the opposite: one who buys in Tyre from storehouses is obligated and from donkey-drivers is exempt, and in Sidon from storehouses is exempt and from donkey-drivers is obligated; therefore some emended the Rambam according to the Tosefta's text (see Tosefta ki-Fshutah, Demai p. 198).
a merchant. Who does not sell what grows in his own fields but buys from others and sells.

if the merchant was a gentile who buys from an Israelite, his produce is demai. For produce bought from an Israelite became obligated in terumot and tithes while with him, and it is not known whether he separated tithes for it properly.

when most of the Land of Israel was in the hands of Israelites, one who bought from any gentile merchant tithed as demai. For it is reasonable to assume that the merchant bought the produce from an Israelite.
and repeated and did it a third time. He brought a second and third time.
even if he brought three loads at once. He brought in one trip the amount that is usually brought in three separate trips.
or he and his son and a laborer brought. Each of whom brought the amount usually brought in one trip.
the merchant has not yet been established. And his produce has the law of a gentile's produce (see Hilchot Terumot 1:10-11).

they did not decree on produce from outside the Land that entered the Land. If it was fixed for tithes in the Land of Israel it is obligated in tithes rabbinically. But they did not decree demai on it (Radbaz, and see Hilchot Terumot 1:22).
produce of the Land that is more plentiful than that of outside the Land. One who buys from the market in a place where most of the produce is from the Land of Israel.
these are subject to demai. Even in Syria (see above, halakhah 4).
and likewise things whose presumption is that they come regularly from outside the Land. That it is customary to bring them from outside the Land.
and darmaskaniyot. A kind of plum that grows around Damascus (explanation of the Tosefta, Lieberman edition, Demai 1:9).
these are exempt from demai. Even in the Land of Israel. For we follow the majority, whether to be lenient or strict (Radbaz).

the Sages did not follow, regarding produce of outside the Land, the appearance, the taste or the smell. When there is doubt whether certain produce is from the Land of Israel or from outside the Land, and it is recognizable by appearance, taste or smell that the produce is from outside the Land, one does not rely on that to exempt it from tithes (but one does follow color, as above, halakhah 5; Tosefta ki-Fshutah, Demai p. 238; some say that only with rice, where the difference is most evident, do we follow appearance; Aruch ha-Shulchan 114:15).
wherever they are plentiful for him. In the very place where the produce is found, as explained in the adjacent paragraph.
permitted. And exempt from tithes.
and where they are not plentiful for him it is forbidden. And he must tithe it as demai.
plentiful in the city. Most of the produce sold in the city is from outside the Land.
but not in the district. For in the villages around the city most of the produce is from the Land of Israel (Chazon Ish, Demai 4:9).
plentiful for the shopkeeper. One who sells in a shop.
and not plentiful for the householder. One who sells in his house.
flour for hides. To use the flour for tanning hides.
for a poultice. To chew and place on a wound for medicine (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 1:8).
for a compress. A piece of cloth smeared with ointment and placed on a wound (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 10:13).

wine for eye salve. A medicine for the eye (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 8:1). In all the things listed so far they did not decree, because by Torah law only something designated for eating, drinking, and anointing is obligated in tithes. Something designated for other use is obligated rabbinically, and where the obligation is rabbinic they did not make the decree of demai (Mishnah Rishonah, Demai 1:3).
and the challah of an ignoramus. Whether the ignoramus separated challah from his own dough, or bought dough from an ignoramus and separated challah from it (Rikevo and other commentators).

and the medumma. Demai produce of chullin into which terumah fell and there is no more than a hundred times the terumah, and one must treat the mixture with the law of terumah. And the ignoramus says he separated tithes from the chullin.
and what is bought with second tithe money. Food bought in Jerusalem from an ignoramus with second tithe money.
and the remains of the meal offerings. The parts of a meal offering eaten by priests, from an offering brought by an ignoramus.
and the addition to the first fruits. Fruits added to the first fruits to increase them, brought by an ignoramus.
all these are exempt from demai. For they did not decree demai on things eaten by priests or in the fulfillment of a mitzvah (Mishnah Rishonah and Tosafot Yom Tov there).
one who buys produce for eating and changed his mind about it for animals. He bought produce to eat and regretted it, and now wants to feed it to animals.
until he rectifies them as demai. For they became obligated in demai when he took them for eating.
fragrant oil. Oil mixed with spices and herbs to give it a pleasant scent.
for its presumption is not for eating. But for smelling (Shenot Eliyahu, Demai 1:3).
oil that the carder takes to put on the wool. To soften the wool and make carding easier. And he is exempt, like one who takes oil to anoint vessels, above, halakhah 14.
but if the weaver takes it to anoint his fingers. To protect them as they rub against the threads.
he is obligated in demai because it is absorbed in his body. And he is like one who anointed oil on his body.
and anointing is like drinking everywhere. See Hilchot Terumot 11:1.
a board. A plank.
to roll on it. To roll on it and thereby anoint his body.

once it has stood, it is permitted for an Israelite to sit after it. For the prohibition of tevel is because of the terumah mixed in it, and just as with terumah an Israelite is permitted to benefit from the oil after a priest has already anointed from it because it has been desacralized (see Hilchot Terumot 11:8 and the explanation there), so too here the terumah in the tevel has already been desacralized by the gentile (Aruch ha-Shulchan 115:11; explanation of the Tosefta, Lieberman edition, Demai 1:22 and Terumot 10:10).

he rubs it and need not be concerned. Because he does not intend to benefit from it (Aruch ha-Shulchan 115:11). Some explain that when the oil fell on his flesh the holiness of the terumah in it was desacralized (Rambam la-Am).
one who buys wine for muries. He buys wine to put into fish brine.
or for alunit. A drink mixed with wine.
tichinin. A kind of cookie made of ground legumes mixed with honey and spices.
is obligated in demai. For he became obligated to tithe when he bought, even if from the time of purchase he intended to make it part of a mixture.
but one who buys muries that has wine in it, etc.. If at the time he bought, the demai was no longer in its own form but mixed, he is exempt from tithing, for they did not decree on a mixture.
since their taste is noticeable. Perceptible throughout the mixture.
all of these that are exempt from demai, for they did not decree on them. As explained above, halakhah 14.
if he rectified them as demai. He rectified them the way one rectifies demai.
what he did is done. And he must bring the second tithe up to Jerusalem and give the terumat ma'aser to a priest.

but if he rectified the demai as certain produce and separated from it terumah gedolah and tithes. If he separated terumah gedolah from demai, the separation does not take effect, since the ignoramus already separated terumah.
or rectified the certain produce as demai. If from certain tevel produce he separated only terumat ma'aser and second tithe.
he did nothing. The produce is not rectified because he did not separate terumah gedolah (Kesef Mishneh, and see Merkevet ha-Mishneh).
the whole city sells certain produce. Produce that is certainly not tithed.
and one sells demai. From which terumah gedolah was already separated.
he separates terumah. Lest he bought from one who sells certain produce, and gives it to a priest (see above 9:5 on the views).
and terumat ma'aser. For whether the produce is certain or demai, it is obligated in terumat ma'aser.

and separates only second tithe. But as to first tithe and poor man's tithe, it is doubtful whether he must give them as for certain produce or only name them as for demai. Therefore he is exempt from giving, by the law of a monetary doubt where the one who would extract from his fellow bears the burden of proof (above 9:2).

and it is like second tithe of demai. Which is treated with certain leniencies, such as that he does not add a fifth if he redeems it, and he is not obligated to remove it (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:4, 11:8).
baskets. Baskets.
he separates from the second, etc.. For the basket that remains is a doubtful tevel.

the wholesaler. A merchant who buys from many people and sells in large quantities. This refers to an ignoramus wholesaler (Rash"s on the Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 5:5; Aruch ha-Shulchan 116:2; and see Rikevo and Radbaz, who explained that it refers to a chaver wholesaler who was permitted to sell demai, as above 11:2).
even from one basket. That he took merchandise from the same basket he took from the first time.
even though he recognizes the barrel to be the same one. The same barrel from which he took the first time.

and this which he took last from a chaver whose produce is rectified. That the wholesaler bought it from a chaver and the produce is tithed. Although he recognizes the barrel, he cannot tithe from this for that, for it is the practice of wholesale sellers to transfer merchandise from barrel to barrel (Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 5:5).
and we have already explained. Above 1:6, Hilchot Terumot 5:12.
and if the wholesaler said, “it is from one person,” he is believed. For although they did not trust him regarding tithes, he is not suspected of lying in this matter.
cucumbers. Cucumbers.
and they bring and pile before him. Those from whom the wholesaler buys pile the vegetables before him in heaps.

the one who buys from him tithes from each cucumber and each cucumber. Because when they pile it before him, it is common for cucumbers or vegetables from different growers to get mixed, some of whom tithe and some of whom do not. And in the previous halakhah it spoke of things that the wholesaler customarily buys separately from each seller, and therefore he may tithe on everything he bought at once.

and from each bundle and bundle. Of vegetables. And he need not tithe from each stalk, because each bundle arrives whole from one grower and there is no concern that the bundles were untied and the vegetables mixed.
one who buys from a householder. Who sells from the produce of his fields (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 5:7) and whose practice is to sell at his house or at the side of his field.
and even from two towns. That each time he bought from him in a different town.

for his presumption is that he sells only from his own. And therefore all his produce has the same law (tithed or untithed), and there is no concern that he separates from the obligated for the exempt.
a householder. Who has his own fields.
who sold vegetables in the market. Who regularly engages in selling in the market like wholesalers, and there is concern that he also sells from others'.
when they bring to him from his gardens, he tithes from one for all. The buyer from him tithes on all the produce together, like one who buys from a householder.
and when they bring to him from other gardens, etc.. His law is that of the wholesaler mentioned in halakhah 1.
the baker. Who kneads the flour and bakes the bread (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 5:4).
he should not tithe from the hot for the cold. From hot, fresh bread for cold bread, which presumably was baked a day earlier.

for I say yesterday's wheat was from one person and today's from another. For it is the baker's practice to buy wheat from different people, and there is concern that the wheat he used yesterday for the cold bread and the wheat he used today for the hot bread came from different people, only one of whom tithes, and one may not separate from the exempt for the obligated (compare Hilchot Bikkurim 6:1).
the retailer. A person who buys from the baker and sells to others (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 5:4).
even though there are many molds. For the bread is made in molds that differ from one another.

tithes from one for all. Because it is the retailer's practice to take from only one baker, and this refers to a case where all the bread was made on the same day and all of it is hot or cold (Kesef Mishneh).

for the baker who sells to the manpol makes his dough in many molds. The fact that the bread is made in different shapes does not indicate that it was bought from different bakers, because sometimes a single baker bakes bread in different molds, for example when he wants to sell to a manpol, a large merchant who wants varied merchandise, so he bakes for him different kinds of bread.
the manpol. A bread seller who buys from two or more bakers.
tithes from each mold and mold. He tithes separately for all the loaves made in the same mold.
for the manpol buys from two bakers. And it is possible that each mold was taken from a different baker.
nine manpolim who buy from ten bakers, etc.. And he bought from one of them and does not know whether the manpol who sold to him bought from one baker or two.

since one of them buys from two, etc.. Since there are more bakers than sellers, it is certain that one of the sellers buys from two bakers and has the law of a manpol, and we are concerned about each and every seller that he may be the one who buys from two.
one who takes from the poor man. Who receives from various people.

and likewise the poor man to whom they gave slices of bread or portions of pressed figs. Pieces cut from a lump of crushed, pressed-together figs. And he wants to rectify, although he was permitted to eat demai (above 10:11).
tithes from each and every one. Perhaps one is tithed and one is not.
and with dried figs. Dried figs.
he mixes everything and tithes. He mixes and tithes from the mixture. Because it involves great effort to tithe from each and every one (Rabbi Ch. Albeck, Demai 5:5).
when the gift is large. That he received a large quantity from each one, and it is possible that the giver already separated tithe.

but with a small gift he tithes from each gift and gift. For with a small gift one can see that the giver is stingy and may not have tithed at all. And if he separates from this for that, he is separating from demai for certain produce, and this is forbidden (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 5:5).
he ground the bread. That he received from various people.
and the dried figs and made them a pressed fig cake. By grinding, honey comes out of them and they stick together and become one lump (Tosefta ki-Fshutah, Demai p. 253).
tithes from one for all. Because he cannot separate for each fig cake and bread by itself, since they have already mixed.
and they left slices. And he wants to eat from the leftovers.
tithes from each and every one. Since it is possible that some were tithed and some not.
